title: Time Series Analysis
text:
A time series is any sequence of measurements taken at regular, equally spaced intervals—seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, quarters, or years. Common examples include weather (daily temperature or rainfall), financial markets (daily stock prices or returns), industry indicators (monthly production or sales), electricity demand, traffic counts, and hospital admissions. In time-series analysis we study how these values evolve: their level, trend, seasonal or calendar patterns (e.g., weekdays vs. weekends, holiday effects), cycles, and anomalies. Typical goals are to describe behavior clearly, forecast future values, and quantify the impact of events or policies.
Because observations are ordered in time, nearby points tend to be correlated (autocorrelation). This violates the independent-and-identically-distributed assumption behind many standard statistical methods, so naïve cross-sectional tools often mislead. Time-series work must explicitly handle dependence, trend, and seasonality—for example by differencing, seasonal adjustment, and models that use lagged values and errors (e.g., ARIMA/SARIMA, ARIMAX/SARIMAX with external drivers, VAR for multiple series, state-space/ETS, or GARCH when volatility changes over time). Analysts also watch for structural breaks (e.g., policy shifts, COVID), outliers, and missing periods, and they evaluate models with time-aware validation (rolling or blocked splits) rather than random shuffles.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
text:
“Eggs at $4? Gas over $5? Rent jumped—again.”
On a chilly morning in early 2023, a grocery receipt went viral: the total looked ordinary, but line items told a story—eggs doubled from a year earlier, milk and bread were up, and a short drive across town now cost noticeably more. That receipt captured what many households felt: inflation isn’t abstract—it shows up in carts, bills, and budgets.
This project asks a simple question with complex answers: How does inflation transmit into the everyday cost of living in the United States—across food, housing, utilities, transportation, and beyond—over time?

title: Introduction
text:
Angles & Candidate Time-Series Sources

1) Food Costs (at home vs away from home)
What to study: Size/timing of pass-through; category heterogeneity; energy & wage channels.
Sources: - BLS CPI: Food at home, Food away from home (monthly) - USDA ERS: Food Price Outlook (monthly narrative & tables) - EIA retail fuel & energy prices (weekly/monthly) - BLS CES: industry hourly earnings (monthly)


2) Shelter Costs (rent, OER, market rents)
What to study: CPI shelter’s stickiness; market rent → CPI lags; mortgage rate environment.
Sources: - BLS CPI: Shelter, Rent of primary residence, Owners’ equivalent rent - Zillow/Apartment List Rent Index (monthly) | Apartment List - Freddie Mac PMMS mortgage rates (weekly) - S&P/Case-Shiller Home Price (monthly)


3) Utilities & Home Energy (electricity, gas, water/sewer/trash)
What to study: Seasonal structure; energy shocks; weather load (HDD/CDD).
Sources: - BLS CPI: Electricity, Utility (piped) gas service, Water/sewer/trash - EIA: retail electricity & natural gas prices/consumption - NOAA: HDD/CDD and temperature time series


4) Transportation & Fuel (gasoline, transit, auto services)
What to study: Oil → gasoline pass-through; asymmetry (rocket-feather); service costs.
Sources: - BLS CPI: Gasoline, Transportation services (e.g., insurance, maintenance) - EIA: WTI/Brent, retail gasoline (weekly) - BLS PPI for upstream costs


5) Household Services (childcare, health out-of-pocket, education, internet/phone)
What to study: Price stickiness; trend vs cyclical; income sensitivity.
Sources: - BLS CPI detailed services (monthly) - FRED health/education price indexes


6) Regional & Demographic Heterogeneity
What to study: Metro/regional CPI; urban vs non-urban; distributional burden.
Sources: - BLS regional CPI & selected metro indexes - BEA regional price parity (annual with trend context) - CPS micro indicators (for demographic overlays)


7) Expectations & Sentiment
What to study: Do inflation expectations predict category moves?
Sources: - NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (monthly) - University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers - Market-based inflation compensation (breakevens via FRED)


8) Supply Chains & Commodities
What to study: Import prices, shipping costs, ag/industrial commodities → retail.
Sources: - BLS Import/Export Price Indexes - FAO Food Price Index - Freight indices (e.g., Drewry/FBX—if accessible)


9) Policy Episodes & Regime Shifts (e.g., COVID-19, tightening cycles)
What to study: Before/after analyses, breaks, and time-varying pass-through.
Sources: - Federal Reserve monetary policy timeline - Fiscal policy events (Treasury/Congressional sources) - CPI category histories (BLS)


10) Forecasts & Scenarios (12–24 months)
What to study: Conditional paths: if core inflation/energy follows a path, where do costs go?
Sources: - Consensus forecasts (e.g., Survey of Professional Forecasters) - EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook - Internal model outputs (produced later)


11) Budget Burden & Distribution (who bears the pain)
What to study: Expenditure shares and effective inflation by group.
Sources: - BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey (annual/quarterly detail) - CPI weights and category shares


12) Nowcasting & High-Frequency Signals (optional)
What to study: Weekly/daily signals that anticipate monthly CPI subcomponents.
Sources: - EIA weekly fuel - Card-type or scanner data if accessible - Web-scraped price indicators (methodology-dependent)

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
section: Food prices: pass-through, lags, and inputs
text:
Food prices: pass-through, lags, and inputs
Retail food inflation typically shows incomplete and lagged pass-through from upstream shocks; energy and labor costs often matter more than raw farm commodities at the shelf. USDA’s Food Price Outlook documents pandemic-era supply disruptions, disease shocks (e.g., HPAI for eggs), and category-specific timing, providing monthly CPI/PPI series and clear event windows that motivate distributed-lag modeling by category (USDA Economic Research Service 2025). Recent Federal Reserve research quantifies U.S. farm-to-retail pass-through magnitudes and delays, offering priors for our ARDL/local-projection specifications and a benchmark for cross-category heterogeneity (Scott, Lusomparodziewicz, and Cowley 2024).

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
section: Shelter: stickiness and measured lags between market rents and CPI
text:
Shelter: stickiness and measured lags between market rents and CPI
A central result is that CPI shelter responds with multi-month lags to movements in market rents due to lease terms, renewal smoothing, and rent-sample design. Ball (2025) formalizes mechanisms that reconcile diverging paths of private rent indices and CPI shelter during 2022–2024. Practitioner analyses reach similar conclusions, stressing persistence risks and the role of market-rent leading indicators (Zillow Research 2025; Roosevelt Institute 2025). These findings motivate our empirical design in which private rent indexes lead CPI shelter; we estimate lag lengths and persistence and run pre/post-COVID stability checks.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
text:
Transportation fuels: asymmetric “rockets and feathers”
The oil-to-gasoline pass-through literature documents asymmetry—pump prices rise faster than they fall (“rockets and feathers”). U.S. studies report regional variation and nonlinearity, implying state-dependent responses we address with threshold/interaction terms or quantile-based local projections (Blair and Ruf 2017; Cook 2019). We apply asymmetric diagnostics to gasoline CPI, embedding crude or wholesale gasoline as drivers along with controls for taxes and seasonality.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
section: Utilities and home energy: weather, seasonality, and energy channels
text:
Utilities and home energy: weather, seasonality, and energy channels
Household electricity and piped gas costs are strongly seasonal and weather-sensitive; heating/cooling degree days (HDD/CDD) are standard predictors of load and bills (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2024; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2021). We incorporate HDD/CDD into seasonal decompositions (STL/X-11) and into monthly ARDLs for electricity and gas service CPI, testing interactions with fuel prices.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
section: Supply chains, COVID-era regimes, and policy episodes
text:
Supply chains, COVID-era regimes, and policy episodes
Pandemic-era inflation featured a regime shift: in 2021 global supply-chain shocks dominated, while by 2022 traditional demand/supply forces reasserted importance; monetary policy appears more effective after bottlenecks eased (National Bureau of Economic Research 2024; Bai et al. 2024). We therefore run structural-break tests, estimate regime-dependent pass-through, and annotate policy windows (e.g., rapid tightening cycles) across categories.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
section: Trade, import prices, and the dollar
text:
Trade, import prices, and the dollar
Global evidence shows the U.S. dollar plays a dominant role in pricing and transmission. A 1% dollar appreciation predicts a sizable decline in global trade volumes within a year, with high pass-through into import prices; currency-of-invoicing frameworks further explain muted exchange-rate pass-through to U.S. consumer prices when imports are dollar-priced (Boz, Gopinath, and Plagborg-Møller 2017; Gopinath, Itskhoki, and Rigobon 2016; Cavallo et al. 2021). For our angles we treat dollar moves and import price inflation as external drivers for traded-goods categories (e.g., gasoline, durables), distinguishing border vs. retail pass-through.

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
text:
Expectations and sentiment
Household and firm inflation expectations influence near-term price dynamics and can amplify persistence. Recent surveys and syntheses highlight channels via which expectations respond to macro/news and, in turn, affect spending and pricing decisions; we include expectations as covariates in nowcasting and short-horizon prediction for selected CPI subcomponents (Coibion, Gorodnichenko, and Weber 2022; Federal Reserve Bank of New York 2025).

title: Inflation in Real Life: Time-Series Insights on U.S. Cost of Living
text:
Regional and distributional perspectives
Regional price parities (RPPs) allow comparisons of price levels across U.S. states/metros, while real personal income series support regional purchasing-power narratives (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis 2024). On the household side, the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE) provides expenditure shares and microdata for distribution-aware analysis, and recent summaries document inflation differences by income during 2021–2023 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2024, 2023). These sources support panel and distributional modeling of burden by region and demographic group.

title: Introduction
section: How this literature shapes our models and angles
text:
How this literature shapes our models and angles

Food. Use ARDL/local projections with energy & wage drivers and category-specific lags; compare pass-through strengths pre/post COVID following ERS and Fed evidence. :contentReferenceoaicite:8

Shelter. Treat market-rent indexes as leaders for CPI shelter; estimate lag structure and persistence per Ball (2025); stress regime/break tests. :contentReferenceoaicite:9

Transportation. Test asymmetric (rocket/feather) pass-through from crude/wholesale to retail gasoline using threshold ARDL or state interactions. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

Utilities. Include HDD/CDD in STL/X-11 decompositions and ARDLs for electricity/gas CPI; evaluate energy price channels. :contentReferenceoaicite:11

Supply-chain/Policy. Implement breaks/regimes and annotate policy cycles consistent with NBER results on 2021–2022 shifts. :contentReferenceoaicite:12

Trade/Dollar. Use dollar/import price drivers selectively for traded-goods categories; distinguish border vs retail pass-through. :contentReferenceoaicite:13

Distribution/Regions. Combine CPI category paths with CE expenditure weights and RPPs to assess burden by income/region. :contentReferenceoaicite:14

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Food represents the most immediate and unavoidable component of household cost of living. Unlike discretionary expenses that can be deferred or eliminated, food consumption is fixed—families must eat regardless of price levels. This makes food inflation uniquely impactful on household budgets, particularly for lower-income families who allocate 15-20% of their income to food compared to 10-12% for higher-income households.
The 2010-2024 period captured in this analysis spans a fundamental transition in American food affordability. What began as a decade of predictable, manageable price increases transformed into the most rapid food cost acceleration in forty years. For households operating on fixed or slowly-growing incomes, this wasn’t an abstract economic statistic—it was the difference between filling a grocery cart for $100 versus $130, between weekly restaurant meals becoming monthly luxuries, between comfortable budgeting and constant financial stress.
The time series analysis that follows dissects this transformation through multiple lenses: trend identification reveals the structural break at COVID-19; autocorrelation analysis confirms price increases are permanent rather than reversible; decomposition shows trend dominance over seasonality; and stationarity tests prove each inflation shock resets the baseline permanently higher. Together, these technical findings translate to a simple household reality: food costs won’t return to pre-pandemic levels, budget adjustments must be permanent, and the middle-class consumption patterns of 2019 now require upper-middle-class incomes in 2024.

theme_set(theme_minimal() +

    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10)
  ))

# Load data function
load_fred_csv <- function(file_path, series_name) {

  tryCatch({
    data <- read_csv(file_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
    
    # Handle different CSV formats
    col_names <- names(data)
    date_col <- col_names[grepl("DATE|date|Date", col_names)][1]
    if (is.na(date_col)) date_col <- col_names[1]
    value_col <- col_names[!col_names %in% date_col][1]
    
    data <- data %>% 
      select(date = all_of(date_col), value = all_of(value_col)) %>%
      mutate(
        date = as.Date(date),
        value = as.numeric(as.character(value))
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(value)) %>%
      arrange(date)
    
    return(data)
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("✗ Error loading", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
    return(NULL)
  })
}

# Load the three CSV files
food_data_files <- list(
  list(path = "data/CUSR0000SAF11.csv", name = "Food at Home CPI", var_name = "food_at_home"),
  list(path = "data/CUSR0000SEFV.csv", name = "Food Away from Home CPI", var_name = "food_away_home"),
  list(path = "data/CPIAUCSL.csv", name = "Overall CPI", var_name = "cpi_all")
)

# Load and combine data
loaded_data <- list()
for (i in 1:length(food_data_files)) {
  file_info <- food_data_files[[i]]
  
  if (file.exists(file_info$path)) {
    data <- load_fred_csv(file_info$path, file_info$name)
    if (!is.null(data)) {
      data <- data %>% rename(!!file_info$var_name := value)
      loaded_data[[file_info$var_name]] <- data
    }
  }
}

# Combine datasets
combined_food_data <- loaded_data[[1]]
for (i in 2:length(loaded_data)) {
  combined_food_data <- combined_food_data %>%
    full_join(loaded_data[[i]], by = "date")
}

# Clean and prepare data
combined_food_data <- combined_food_data %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  filter(if_any(-date, ~ !is.na(.x)))

# TIME SERIES PLOTS AND COMPONENT IDENTIFICATION

# Create time series objects
create_ts_objects <- function(data) {
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  ts_list <- list()
  
  # Determine start date and frequency
  start_year <- year(min(data$date))
  start_month <- month(min(data$date))
  
  for (col in available_cols) {
    ts_list[[col]] <- ts(data[[col]], start = c(start_year, start_month), frequency = 12)
  }
  
  return(ts_list)
}

ts_data <- create_ts_objects(combined_food_data)

# Function to analyze time series components
analyze_ts_components <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  # Convert to data frame for ggplot
  ts_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )
  
  # Create comprehensive time series plot
  p <- ggplot(ts_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, color = "#ff7f0e", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Time Series Analysis:", series_name),
      subtitle = "Blue line: Original series | Orange line: Trend (LOESS smoothing)",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Consumer Price Index",
      caption = "Data: Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2020-03-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.6) +
    annotate("text", x = as.Date("2020-06-01"), y = max(ts_df$value) * 0.95, 
             label = "COVID-19", color = "red", size = 3, angle = 90) 
  
  return(p)
}

# Create time series plots for each variable
available_vars <- names(ts_data)
ts_plots <- list()

for (i in 1:length(available_vars)) {
  var_name <- available_vars[i]
  display_name <- case_when(
    var_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    var_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    var_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(var_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  ts_plots[[i]] <- analyze_ts_components(ts_data[[var_name]], display_name)
  print(ts_plots[[i]])
}























These time series demonstrate a clear structural break at the COVID-19 pandemic. Pre-2020 food prices followed stable, predictable growth patterns of roughly 2-3% annually. Post-2020, all categories accelerated sharply—groceries increased 30% in four years, equivalent to a decade of pre-pandemic inflation compressed into half the time.
The “Food Away from Home” series shows the steepest and most persistent acceleration, driven by labor market pressures in service industries. The narrowing gap between grocery and restaurant inflation is significant: it eliminated the traditional household buffer of substituting home cooking for dining out during inflationary periods.
What makes this particularly impactful is the synchronization across categories. When food, housing, and energy inflate simultaneously—as shown in the Overall CPI—households cannot offset one expense by reducing another. Lower-income households, which allocate larger budget shares to food, face the greatest pressure with the least flexibility to adjust. The data indicates this is not a temporary price shock but a regime shift. The smooth post-pandemic trajectories suggest inflation became embedded in pricing mechanisms and wage structures. This created sustained real income erosion that required both household behavioral adjustment and monetary policy intervention to address.





Show Code
# LAG PLOTS ANALYSIS
library(forecast)

# Create lag plots for each series
for (i in 1:length(available_vars)) {
  var_name <- available_vars[i]
  display_name <- case_when(
    var_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    var_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI", 
    var_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(var_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  # Create lag plot using gglagplot
  lag_plot <- gglagplot(ts_data[[var_name]], lags = 16,do.lines=FALSE) +
    ggtitle(paste("Lag Plots Analysis:", display_name)) +
    xlab("Lagged Values") +
    ylab("Current Values") +
    theme_bw()
  
  print(lag_plot)
}























All three CPI series exhibit extremely strong positive autocorrelation across all lag periods, as evidenced by the tight clustering of points along the diagonal reference lines. This pattern reveals several key insights:
The high persistence at lag 1 confirms that food prices are highly predictable in the short term—this month’s prices closely predict next month’s. This autocorrelation remains strong even at lag 12, indicating minimal seasonal variation in food inflation. Unlike agricultural commodities that show clear seasonal patterns, processed food CPIs demonstrate smooth, trend-dominated behavior.
The structural break is visible in the color gradients, particularly in “Food at Home” CPI. Points deviate further from the reference line at higher lags (13-16), reflecting the post-pandemic acceleration that disrupted historical price relationships. The pandemic created a regime shift where past values became less reliable predictors of future values. “Food Away from Home” shows the most consistent linearity across all lags, suggesting restaurant prices follow an almost mechanical upward trajectory with minimal volatility. This reflects sticky pricing in service industries where menu adjustments occur infrequently but persistently.
From a household perspective, this strong autocorrelation means food price increases are highly predictable but non-reversible. Unlike energy prices that can spike and retreat, food inflation exhibits a ratchet effect—prices rise and stay elevated. This creates sustained purchasing power erosion rather than temporary shocks, making budget adjustment particularly challenging for households.

# TIME SERIES DECOMPOSITION
decomposition_results <- list()

for (i in 1:length(available_vars)) {
  var_name <- available_vars[i]
  display_name <- case_when(
    var_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    var_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    var_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(var_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  # Try multiplicative first
  tryCatch({
    decomp_mult <- decompose(ts_data[[var_name]], type = "multiplicative")
    
    # Create plot using autoplot
    p <- autoplot(decomp_mult) +
      ggtitle(paste("Time Series Decomposition:", display_name)) +
      labs(subtitle = "Decomposition Type: Multiplicative",
           x = "Time",
           y = "Value") 
      theme_bw() +
      theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
    
    print(p)
    decomposition_results[[var_name]] <- list(decomposition = decomp_mult, type = "multiplicative")

    
  }, error = function(e) {
    # Try additive if multiplicative fails
    cat("Multiplicative failed, trying additive for", display_name, "\n")
    
    tryCatch({
      decomp_add <- decompose(ts_data[[var_name]], type = "additive")
      
      # Create plot using autoplot

create_acf_pacf_analysis <- function(ts_obj, series_name, max_lag = 36) {
  
  # Calculate ACF and PACF
  acf_result <- acf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  pacf_result <- pacf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  
  # Create ACF data frame
  acf_df <- data.frame(

    acf = acf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "ACF (Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Create PACF data frame  
  pacf_df <- data.frame(
    lag = pacf_result$lag[,,1],
    acf = pacf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Combine data
  combined_df <- rbind(acf_df, pacf_df)
  
  # Calculate confidence intervals
  n <- length(ts_obj)
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +

    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Autocorrelation Analysis:", series_name),
      subtitle = "ACF and PACF plots for stationarity and model identification",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Dashed blue lines: 95% confidence intervals | Values outside indicate significant correlation"

      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    ) +

  return(list(plot = p, acf_values = acf_result, pacf_values = pacf_result))
}

# AUGMENTED DICKEY-FULLER STATIONARITY TESTS

perform_adf_tests <- function(ts_data, series_names) {
  
  adf_results <- data.frame(
    Series = character(),
    ADF_Statistic = numeric(),
    P_Value = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_1pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_5pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_10pct = numeric(),
    Is_Stationary_5pct = logical(),
    Is_Stationary_1pct = logical(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  cat("Performing ADF tests...\n")
  
  for(i in 1:length(series_names)) {
    series_name <- series_names[i]
    ts_obj <- ts_data[[series_name]]
    
    # Clean data more thoroughly
    ts_numeric <- as.numeric(ts_obj)  # Convert to numeric first
    ts_clean <- ts_numeric[!is.na(ts_numeric) & is.finite(ts_numeric)]  # Remove NA and infinite values
    
    # Check if we have enough data points
    if (length(ts_clean) < 10) {
      cat("✗ Insufficient data for", series_name, "(", length(ts_clean), "valid points)\n")
      next
    }
    
    # Perform ADF test
    tryCatch({
      adf_test <- adf.test(ts_clean, alternative = "stationary")
      
      display_name <- case_when(
        series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
        series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
        series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
        TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
      )
      
      # Extract critical values properly
      critical_values <- adf_test$parameter
      if (is.null(critical_values) || length(critical_values) == 0) {
        # Use standard critical values if not available
        crit_1pct <- -3.43
        crit_5pct <- -2.86
        crit_10pct <- -2.57
      } else {
        crit_1pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 1, critical_values[1], -3.43)
        crit_5pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 2, critical_values[2], -2.86)
        crit_10pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 3, critical_values[3], -2.57)
      }
      
      adf_results <<- rbind(adf_results, data.frame(
        Series = display_name,
        ADF_Statistic = round(adf_test$statistic, 4),
        P_Value = round(adf_test$p.value, 4),
        Critical_Value_1pct = round(crit_1pct, 4),
        Critical_Value_5pct = round(crit_5pct, 4), 
        Critical_Value_10pct = round(crit_10pct, 4),
        Is_Stationary_5pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.05,
        Is_Stationary_1pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.01
      ))
      
      cat("✓", display_name, "- ADF Statistic:", round(adf_test$statistic, 4), 
          ", p-value:", round(adf_test$p.value, 4), 
          ", Stationary (5%):", adf_test$p.value < 0.05, "\n")
      
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("✗ Error testing", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
      
      # Print diagnostic info
      cat("   Data type:", class(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data length:", length(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data range:", paste(round(range(ts_clean, na.rm = TRUE), 2), collapse = " to "), "\n")
      cat("   First few values:", paste(head(ts_clean, 5), collapse = ", "), "\n")
    })
  }
  
  return(adf_results)
}

make_stationary <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI", 
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )

  # First differencing
  diff1 <- diff(ts_obj, differences = 1)
  
  # Test stationarity of differenced series
  adf_test_diff1 <- adf.test(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], alternative = "stationary")
  
  # Create comparison plots - Original vs First Difference
  original_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj),
    series_type = "Original Series"
  )
  
  diff1_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(diff1)),
    value = as.numeric(diff1),
    series_type = "First Difference"
  )
  
  combined_df <- rbind(original_df, diff1_df)
  
  p1 <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Stationarity Transformation:", display_name),
      subtitle = paste("First difference ADF p-value:", round(adf_test_diff1$p.value, 4)),
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value",
      caption = "First differencing removes trend to achieve stationarity"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    )
  
  # ACF comparison - Original vs Differenced
  acf_orig <- acf(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  acf_diff1 <- acf(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  
  acf_orig_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_orig$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_orig$acf[,,1],
    series_type = "Original Series ACF"
  )
  
  acf_diff1_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_diff1$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_diff1$acf[,,1], 
    series_type = "First Difference ACF"
  )
  
  acf_combined <- rbind(acf_orig_df, acf_diff1_df)
  
  n <- length(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)])
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p2 <- ggplot(acf_combined, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("ACF Comparison after Differencing:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparing autocorrelation structure before and after first differencing",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Stationary series should show rapid decay in ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(list(
    comparison_plot = p1,
    acf_comparison = p2,
    differenced_series = diff1,
    adf_result = adf_test_diff1,
    is_stationary_after_diff = adf_test_diff1$p.value < 0.05
  ))
}

    original = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )

  for(window in windows) {
    ma_values <- SMA(ts_obj, n = window)

      ),
      line_type = ifelse(ma_type == "original", "Original", "Smoothed"),
      line_size = ifelse(ma_type == "original", 1.2, 1.0)
    )
  
  p <- ggplot(ma_long, aes(x = date, y = value, color = ma_type_clean, size = line_size)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Series Type", option = "plasma") +
    scale_size_identity() +
    labs(
      title = paste("Moving Average Smoothing Analysis:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparison of different smoothing windows to identify underlying patterns",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Index Value",
      caption = "Different MA windows reveal trend (long MA) vs seasonal patterns (short MA)"

    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)

    guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 3))
  
  return(p)

title: Data Visualization
text:
This comprehensive analysis examines U.S. inflation trends through the lens of everyday American experiences, using Consumer Price Index (CPI) data from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) spanning January 2010 to December 2024. Our investigation begins with food inflation—the most immediate and visceral form of price pressure that families face daily. The original dataset comprises four key food price indices: Food at Home CPI (representing grocery costs), Food Away from Home CPI (restaurant and dining costs), Food Total CPI (aggregate food prices), and Overall CPI (economy-wide price levels). These monthly time series capture approximately 15 years of dining table economics, encompassing multiple economic cycles including the 2008 financial crisis recovery, pre-pandemic stability, COVID-19 disruption, and subsequent policy responses.
Building upon this foundation, we’ve expanded our analysis to encompass the broader landscape of American cost of living through three additional critical dimensions that shape household budgets and financial well-being. Housing costs represent the largest expense for most families, tracked through Shelter CPI (overall housing expenses), Rent CPI (rental market dynamics), and 30-Year Mortgage Rates (the gateway to homeownership). Energy prices, captured through Gasoline CPI, serve as both a direct household expense and a barometer of broader economic volatility that ripples through transportation, goods delivery, and consumer sentiment. Finally, the financial environment—measured by Federal Funds Rate and 10-Year Treasury Rate—reveals how monetary policy decisions in Washington boardrooms ultimately affect family budgets across America.
Together, these indicators weave a story of how abstract economic forces translate into concrete realities: the monthly rent check, the weekly grocery bill, the daily commute, and the long-term dream of homeownership. This multi-dimensional approach captures not just what inflation looks like in government statistics, but how it feels in American households.


Show Code
# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)
library(forecast)
library(tseries)
library(gridExtra)
library(viridis)
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(scales)
library(tidyr)

# Read all CSV files
shelter_cpi <- read_csv("./data/CUSR0000SAH1.csv")
rent_cpi <- read_csv("./data/CUSR0000SEHA.csv")
mortgage_rate <- read_csv("./data/MORTGAGE30US.csv")
gasoline_cpi <- read_csv("./data/CUSR0000SETB01.csv")
treasury_10y <- read_csv("./data/DGS10.csv")
fed_funds <- read_csv("./data/FEDFUNDS.csv")

shelter_cpi$DATE <- as.Date(shelter_cpi$observation_date)
rent_cpi$DATE <- as.Date(rent_cpi$observation_date)
mortgage_rate$DATE <- as.Date(mortgage_rate$observation_date)
gasoline_cpi$DATE <- as.Date(gasoline_cpi$observation_date)
treasury_10y$DATE <- as.Date(treasury_10y$observation_date)
fed_funds$DATE <- as.Date(fed_funds$observation_date)

# Rename value columns for clarity (assuming second column contains values)
names(shelter_cpi)[2] <- "Shelter_CPI"
names(rent_cpi)[2] <- "Rent_CPI"
names(mortgage_rate)[2] <- "Mortgage_Rate"
names(gasoline_cpi)[2] <- "Gasoline_CPI"
names(treasury_10y)[2] <- "Treasury_10Y"
names(fed_funds)[2] <- "Fed_Funds_Rate"

# Set theme
theme_set(theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10)
  ))


# Create data directory
if (!dir.exists("data")) {
  dir.create("data")
  cat("Created 'data' directory\n")
}

# Food-related FRED series IDs 
food_series <- list(
  list(id = "CUSR0000SAF11", name = "Food at Home CPI"),
  list(id = "CUSR0000SEFV", name = "Food Away from Home CPI"),
  list(id = "CUSR0000SAF1", name = "Food and Beverages Total CPI"),
  list(id = "CPIAUCSL", name = "Overall CPI (All Items)")
)

# Download all food-related data
food_data_list <- list()

# Check what data we successfully downloaded
successful_downloads <- names(food_data_list)
for (id in successful_downloads) {
  series_name <- food_series[[which(sapply(food_series, function(x) x$id == id))]]$name
  cat("✓", id, "-", series_name, "\n")
}

# Function to load and clean FRED CSV files
load_fred_csv <- function(file_path, series_name) {

  tryCatch({
    # Read the CSV file
    data <- read_csv(file_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
    
    # Handle different CSV formats from FRED
    if (ncol(data) >= 2) {
      # Check column names and standardize
      col_names <- names(data)
      
      # Find date column
      date_col <- col_names[grepl("DATE|date|Date", col_names)][1]
      if (is.na(date_col)) date_col <- col_names[1]  # First column if no DATE found
      
      # Find value column  
      value_col <- col_names[!col_names %in% date_col][1]  # First non-date column
      
      # Select and rename columns
      data <- data %>% 
        select(date = all_of(date_col), value = all_of(value_col))
      
      # Clean and convert data
      data <- data %>%
        mutate(
          date = as.Date(date),
          value = as.numeric(as.character(value))
        ) %>%
        filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(value), value != ".", !is.infinite(value)) %>%
        arrange(date)
      
      return(data)
    } else {
      cat("✗ Unexpected file format for", series_name, "\n")
      return(NULL)
    }
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("✗ Error loading", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
    return(NULL)
  })
}

# Define the data files we expect
food_data_files <- list(
  list(path = "data/CUSR0000SAF11.csv", name = "Food at Home CPI", var_name = "food_at_home"),
  list(path = "data/CUSR0000SEFV.csv", name = "Food Away from Home CPI", var_name = "food_away_home"),
  list(path = "data/CPIAUCSL.csv", name = "Overall CPI (All Items)", var_name = "cpi_all")
)

# Check for additional files
if (file.exists("data/CUSR0000SAF1.csv")) {
  food_data_files <- append(food_data_files, 
    list(list(path = "data/CUSR0000SAF1.csv", name = "Food and Beverages Total CPI", var_name = "food_total")), 
    after = 2)
}

# Load all available files
loaded_data <- list()
for (i in 1:length(food_data_files)) {
  file_info <- food_data_files[[i]]
  
  if (file.exists(file_info$path)) {
    data <- load_fred_csv(file_info$path, file_info$name)
    if (!is.null(data)) {
      # Rename the value column to the appropriate variable name
      data <- data %>% rename(!!file_info$var_name := value)
      loaded_data[[file_info$var_name]] <- data
    }
  } else {
    cat("File not found:", file_info$path, "\n")
  }
}

# Combine all loaded data
if (length(loaded_data) >= 2) {
  # Start with the first dataset
  combined_food_data <- loaded_data[[1]]
  
  # Join other datasets
  for (i in 2:length(loaded_data)) {
    combined_food_data <- combined_food_data %>%
      full_join(loaded_data[[i]], by = "date")
  }
  
  # If we don't have food_total but have both components, calculate it
  if (!"food_total" %in% names(combined_food_data) && 
      all(c("food_at_home", "food_away_home") %in% names(combined_food_data))) {
    
    combined_food_data <- combined_food_data %>%
      mutate(food_total = (food_at_home + food_away_home) / 2)
  }
  
  # Sort by date and remove rows with all missing values
  combined_food_data <- combined_food_data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    filter(if_any(-date, ~ !is.na(.x)))

  
} else {
  stop("ERROR: Need at least 2 data series to proceed. Please check your data files in the 'data/' folder.")
}

# Summary statistics
data_summary <- combined_food_data %>%
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    date_start = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    date_end = max(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    years_covered = round(as.numeric(difftime(max(date, na.rm = TRUE), min(date, na.rm = TRUE), units = "days")) / 365.25, 1)
  )

# Check completeness for each variable
available_vars <- names(combined_food_data)[names(combined_food_data) != "date"]
completeness <- combined_food_data %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(available_vars), ~ round(sum(!is.na(.x)) / n() * 100, 1), .names = "{.col}_complete"))

title: Data Visualization
text:
Interactive Food Inflation Dashboard
The comprehensive dashboard reveals distinct phases in food price evolution through multiple analytical lenses. The upper left panel displays absolute CPI levels, showing steady upward trajectories with notable acceleration post-2020. Food away from home (orange line) exhibits the steepest price growth, reaching nearly 380 index points by 2024, while food at home (blue line) demonstrates more moderate increases.
The year-over-year inflation rates (upper right) expose the volatile nature of food price changes, with dramatic spikes during 2021-2022 reaching 10-14% annually—levels not observed since the early 1980s. The indexed comparison (lower left) normalizes all series to 100 at the start period, clearly illustrating that restaurant prices have increased approximately 65% compared to 45% for groceries since 2010. The recent three-year trend (lower right) captures the inflation surge and subsequent moderation, with most categories returning toward 2-4% annual growth by late 2024.


Show Code
create_plotly_dashboard <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns (excluding date)
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  # Calculate year-over-year inflation rates
  inflation_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(., 12) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_yoy")
    ) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_yoy"), ~ !is.na(.x)))
  
  # Color palette
  colors <- c('#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c', '#d62728', '#9467bd')
  
  # PLOT 1: Price Index Levels
  p1 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  for (i in seq_along(available_cols)) {
    col_name <- available_cols[i]
    display_name <- case_when(
      col_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home",
      col_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home",
      col_name == "food_total" ~ "Food Total",
      col_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI",
      TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(col_name, "_", " "))
    )
    
    p1 <- p1 %>% 
      add_trace(data = data, x = ~date, y = data[[col_name]], 
                name = display_name,
                line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                     'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                     'Value: %{y:.1f}<br>',
                                     '<extra></extra>'))
  }
  
  p1 <- p1 %>%
    layout(
      title = "Price Index Levels",
      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Index Value"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      shapes = list(
        list(
          type = "line",
          x0 = as.Date("2020-03-01"), x1 = as.Date("2020-03-01"),
          y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
          yref = "paper",
          line = list(color = "red", dash = "dot", width = 1)
        )
      )
    )
  
  # PLOT 2: YoY Inflation Rates
  p2 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  yoy_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_yoy")
  for (i in seq_along(yoy_cols)) {
    col_name <- yoy_cols[i]
    if (col_name %in% names(inflation_data)) {
      orig_name <- available_cols[i]
      display_name <- case_when(
        orig_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home",
        orig_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away",
        orig_name == "food_total" ~ "Food Total",
        orig_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI",
        TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(orig_name, "_", " "))
      )
      
      p2 <- p2 %>% 
        add_trace(data = inflation_data, x = ~date, y = inflation_data[[col_name]], 
                  name = paste(display_name, "YoY%"),
                  line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                  hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                       'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                       'YoY Change: %{y:.1f}%<br>',
                                       '<extra></extra>'))
    }
  }
  
  p2 <- p2 %>%
    layout(
      title = "Year-over-Year Inflation Rates (%)",
      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "YoY % Change"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      shapes = list(
        list(
          type = "line",
          x0 = 0, x1 = 1,
          xref = "paper",
          y0 = 0, y1 = 0,
          line = list(color = "gray", dash = "dash", width = 1)
        ),
        list(
          type = "line",
          x0 = as.Date("2020-03-01"), x1 = as.Date("2020-03-01"),
          y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
          yref = "paper",
          line = list(color = "red", dash = "dot", width = 1)
        )
      )
    )
  
  # PLOT 3: Indexed trends (first value = 100)
  indexed_data <- data %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(available_cols), 
                  ~ (. / first(., na_rm = TRUE)) * 100, 
                  .names = "{.col}_idx"))
  
  p3 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  idx_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_idx")
  for (i in seq_along(idx_cols)) {
    col_name <- idx_cols[i]
    orig_name <- available_cols[i]
    display_name <- case_when(
      orig_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home",
      orig_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away",
      orig_name == "food_total" ~ "Food Total",
      orig_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI",
      TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(orig_name, "_", " "))
    )
    
    p3 <- p3 %>% 
      add_trace(data = indexed_data, x = ~date, y = indexed_data[[col_name]], 
                name = paste(display_name, "(Index)"),
                line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                     'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                     'Index: %{y:.1f}<br>',
                                     '<extra></extra>'))
  }
  
  p3 <- p3 %>%
    layout(
      title = "Cumulative Price Changes (First Value = 100)",
      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Index (Base = 100)"),

Seasonal and Period-Based Inflation Patterns
The heatmap analysis reveals systematic differences across time periods and seasonal patterns. The COVID era (2020-2022) displays predominantly red coloration, indicating sustained high inflation across all food categories throughout most months. This contrasts sharply with the pre-COVID period (2011-2019), characterized by predominantly neutral to mild positive inflation rates. The post-COVID era (2023+) shows a cooling pattern, with inflation rates moderating but remaining elevated compared to historical norms.
Seasonal patterns emerge within each period: food prices typically show modest increases during winter months and more variable behavior during summer periods. The intensity of seasonal effects appears amplified during the COVID era, suggesting that supply chain disruptions interacted with normal seasonal variations to create more pronounced price swings.

# GGPLOT2 Heatmap - Food Inflation Analysis
create_ggplot_heatmap <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  # Calculate year-over-year changes
  heatmap_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(., 12) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_yoy")
    ) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_yoy"), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
    select(date, ends_with("_yoy")) %>%
    mutate(
      year = year(date),
      month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = ends_with("_yoy"), names_to = "category", values_to = "inflation_rate") %>%
    mutate(
      category_clean = case_when(
        category == "food_at_home_yoy" ~ "Food at Home",
        category == "food_away_home_yoy" ~ "Food Away from Home",
        category == "food_total_yoy" ~ "Food Total",
        category == "cpi_all_yoy" ~ "Overall CPI",
        TRUE ~ str_remove(category, "_yoy") %>% str_to_title()
      ),
      period = case_when(
        year <= 2019 ~ "Pre-COVID (2011-2019)",
        year %in% 2020:2022 ~ "COVID Era (2020-2022)",
        year >= 2023 ~ "Post-COVID (2023+)",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(inflation_rate))
  
  if (nrow(heatmap_data) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "Insufficient data for heatmap"))
  }
  
  # Create the heatmap with proper dimensions and clean layout
  g <- ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = month, y = fct_rev(category_clean), fill = inflation_rate)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.8) +
    # Remove ALL text inside tiles for clean appearance
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
      midpoint = 0, name = "YoY %\nChange",
      limits = c(-10, 20), oob = scales::squish,
      breaks = seq(-10, 20, by = 5)
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~ period, ncol = 1, strip.position = "top") +  # Single column layout
    labs(
      title = "Food Inflation Heatmap: Year-over-Year Changes",
      subtitle = "Seasonal patterns across different time periods",
      x = "Month",
      y = "Food Category",
      caption = "Data: Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      # Fix text sizing and spacing
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, angle = 0, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
      
      # Clean facet labels
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.8),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      
      # Title formatting
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
      
      # Legend positioning
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
      
      # Proper spacing
      panel.spacing.y = unit(1.5, "lines"),
      plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
      
      # Remove grid
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    )
  
  return(g)
}

title: Data Visualization
text:
Price Volatility Analysis
The volatility analysis quantifies price uncertainty through rolling 12-month standard deviations of monthly price changes. Food at home (blue line) exhibits the highest volatility throughout most of the analysis period, with dramatic spikes reaching 0.8% monthly volatility during 2020-2021. This represents unprecedented price unpredictability, far exceeding levels observed during the 2008-2009 financial crisis.
The COVID-19 period marks a clear structural break in price stability across all food categories. Pre-pandemic volatility typically ranged between 0.1-0.3% monthly, while post-COVID levels reached 0.4-0.8%. The synchronized increase across all categories suggests systemic rather than category-specific shocks. By 2024, volatility has declined but remains above pre-pandemic baselines, indicating persistent supply chain fragility.


Show Code
create_ggplot_volatility <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  if (length(available_cols) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "No data available for volatility analysis"))
  }
  
  # Calculate price changes and rolling volatility
  volatility_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      # Monthly price changes
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(.) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_change")
    )
  
  # Calculate rolling volatility manually for each change column
  change_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_change")
  
  for (col in change_cols) {
    if (col %in% names(volatility_data)) {
      # Use rollapply instead of rollsd
      volatility_data[[paste0(col, "_vol")]] <- zoo::rollapply(
        volatility_data[[col]], 
        width = 12, 
        FUN = function(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), 
        fill = NA, 
        align = "right",
        partial = FALSE
      )
    }
  }
  
  # Continue with the rest of the analysis
  volatility_data <- volatility_data %>%
    select(date, ends_with("_vol")) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_vol"), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "category", values_to = "volatility") %>%
    mutate(
      category_clean = case_when(
        str_detect(category, "food_at_home") ~ "Food at Home",
        str_detect(category, "food_away_home") ~ "Food Away from Home",
        str_detect(category, "food_total") ~ "Food Total", 
        str_detect(category, "cpi_all") ~ "Overall CPI",
        TRUE ~ str_remove_all(category, "_change_vol") %>% str_to_title()
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(volatility))
  
  if (nrow(volatility_data) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "Insufficient data for volatility analysis"))
  }
  
  # Select colors based on available categories
  n_categories <- length(unique(volatility_data$category_clean))
  colors <- c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd")[1:n_categories]
  
  # Create the volatility plot
  g <- ggplot(volatility_data, aes(x = date, y = volatility, color = category_clean)) +
    geom_line(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colors, name = "Category") +
    labs(
      title = "Food Price Volatility: Rolling 12-Month Standard Deviation",
      subtitle = "Measuring price stability across food categories over time",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Monthly Price Change Volatility (%)",
      caption = "Higher volatility = more unpredictable price changes | Smooth lines show trends"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2020-03-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2008-09-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", alpha = 0.7) +
    annotate("text", x = as.Date("2020-06-01"), y = max(volatility_data$volatility, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.9, 
             label = "COVID-19", color = "red", size = 3.5) 
  
  return(g)
}

# Create and display volatility analysis
ggplot_volatility <- create_ggplot_volatility(combined_food_data)
print(ggplot_volatility)









In terms of the food prices part, the data narrative reveals a three-act inflation story. Act I (2010-2019) represents the “Great Moderation” period with stable, predictable food price growth averaging 1-2% annually. Act II (2020-2022) depicts the “Great Disruption”—unprecedented supply chain shocks, monetary expansion, and demand shifts creating multi-decade high inflation rates. Act III (2023-2024) shows “Gradual Normalization”—inflation cooling but price levels permanently elevated, with volatility settling at new, higher equilibrium levels.
The March 2020 inflection point visible across all visualizations marks when pandemic-induced disruptions transformed food markets. Supply chain bottlenecks, labor shortages, and shifting consumption patterns from restaurants to groceries created sustained inflationary pressures. The differential impact between food at home and away from home reflects these consumption shifts and varying supply chain vulnerabilities.
This demonstrates how external shocks can fundamentally alter inflation dynamics, with effects persisting long after initial disruptions subside. The food sector’s essential nature amplified both the immediate impacts and policy responses, creating feedback loops that sustained elevated price growth well into the recovery period.

Interactive Food Inflation Dashboard
The comprehensive dashboard reveals distinct phases in food price evolution through multiple analytical lenses. The upper left panel displays absolute CPI levels, showing steady upward trajectories with notable acceleration post-2020. Food away from home (orange line) exhibits the steepest price growth, reaching nearly 380 index points by 2024, while food at home (blue line) demonstrates more moderate increases.
The year-over-year inflation rates (upper right) expose the volatile nature of food price changes, with dramatic spikes during 2021-2022 reaching 10-14% annually—levels not observed since the early 1980s. The indexed comparison (lower left) normalizes all series to 100 at the start period, clearly illustrating that restaurant prices have increased approximately 65% compared to 45% for groceries since 2010. The recent three-year trend (lower right) captures the inflation surge and subsequent moderation, with most categories returning toward 2-4% annual growth by late 2024.


Show Code
create_plotly_dashboard <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns (excluding date)
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  # Calculate year-over-year inflation rates
  inflation_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(., 12) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_yoy")
    ) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_yoy"), ~ !is.na(.x)))
  
  # Color palette
  colors <- c('#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c', '#d62728', '#9467bd')
  
  # PLOT 1: Price Index Levels
  p1 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  for (i in seq_along(available_cols)) {
    col_name <- available_cols[i]
    display_name <- case_when(
      col_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home",
      col_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home",
      col_name == "food_total" ~ "Food Total",
      col_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI",
      TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(col_name, "_", " "))
    )
    
    p1 <- p1 %>% 
      add_trace(data = data, x = ~date, y = data[[col_name]], 
                name = display_name,
                line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                     'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                     'Value: %{y:.1f}<br>',
                                     '<extra></extra>'))
  }
  
  p1 <- p1 %>%
    layout(
      title = "Price Index Levels",
      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Index Value"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      shapes = list(
        list(
          type = "line",
          x0 = as.Date("2020-03-01"), x1 = as.Date("2020-03-01"),
          y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
          yref = "paper",
          line = list(color = "red", dash = "dot", width = 1)
        )
      )
    )
  
  # PLOT 2: YoY Inflation Rates
  p2 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  yoy_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_yoy")
  for (i in seq_along(yoy_cols)) {

        orig_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI",

      )
      
      p2 <- p2 %>% 
        add_trace(data = inflation_data, x = ~date, y = inflation_data[[col_name]], 
                  name = paste(display_name, "YoY%"),
                  line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                  hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                       'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                       'YoY Change: %{y:.1f}%<br>',
                                       '<extra></extra>'))
    }
  }
  
  p2 <- p2 %>%
    layout(
      title = "Year-over-Year Inflation Rates (%)",
      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "YoY % Change"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      shapes = list(

          y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
          yref = "paper",
          line = list(color = "red", dash = "dot", width = 1)
        )
      )
    )
  
  # PLOT 3: Indexed trends (first value = 100)
  indexed_data <- data %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(available_cols), 
                  ~ (. / first(., na_rm = TRUE)) * 100, 
                  .names = "{.col}_idx"))
  
  p3 <- plot_ly(type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')
  
  idx_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_idx")
  for (i in seq_along(idx_cols)) {

      add_trace(data = indexed_data, x = ~date, y = indexed_data[[col_name]],

                line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                hovertemplate = paste('<b>', display_name, '</b><br>',
                                     'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                     'Index: %{y:.1f}<br>',
                                     '<extra></extra>'))
  }
  
  p3 <- p3 %>%
    layout(

      xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Index (Base = 100)"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      shapes = list(

  if (nrow(recent_data) > 0) {

                    marker = list(size = 4, color = colors[i]),

                                         'Date: %{x}<br>',
                                         'YoY Change: %{y:.1f}%<br>',
                                         '<extra></extra>'))

    }

  p4 <- p4 %>%

      title = "Recent 3-Year Inflation Trend",

      showlegend = TRUE,

          xref = "paper",
          y0 = 0, y1 = 0,
          line = list(color = "gray", dash = "dash", width = 1)
        )
      )
    )
  combined_plot <- subplot(
    subplot(p1, p2, nrows = 1, shareY = FALSE, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE),
    subplot(p3, p4, nrows = 1, shareY = FALSE, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE),
    nrows = 2, shareX = FALSE, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE,
    heights = c(0.5, 0.5)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "<b>Food Inflation Dashboard: Real CPI Data Analysis</b><br><sup>Interactive analysis of food price trends and inflation rates | Red dashed lines mark COVID-19 onset (March 2020)</sup>",
      font = list(size = 16)
    ),
    template = "plotly_white",
    height = 800,
    showlegend = FALSE
  )
  
  return(combined_plot)
}

Seasonal and Period-Based Inflation Patterns
The heatmap analysis reveals systematic differences across time periods and seasonal patterns. The COVID era (2020-2022) displays predominantly red coloration, indicating sustained high inflation across all food categories throughout most months. This contrasts sharply with the pre-COVID period (2011-2019), characterized by predominantly neutral to mild positive inflation rates. Show Code
# GGPLOT2 Heatmap - Food Inflation Analysis
create_ggplot_heatmap <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  # Calculate year-over-year changes
  heatmap_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(., 12) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_yoy")
    ) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_yoy"), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
    select(date, ends_with("_yoy")) %>%
    mutate(
      year = year(date),
      month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = ends_with("_yoy"), names_to = "category", values_to = "inflation_rate") %>%
    mutate(
      category_clean = case_when(
        category == "food_at_home_yoy" ~ "Food at Home",
        category == "food_away_home_yoy" ~ "Food Away from Home",
        category == "food_total_yoy" ~ "Food Total",
        category == "cpi_all_yoy" ~ "Overall CPI",
        TRUE ~ str_remove(category, "_yoy") %>% str_to_title()
      ),
      period = case_when(
        year <= 2019 ~ "Pre-COVID (2011-2019)",
        year %in% 2020:2022 ~ "COVID Era (2020-2022)",
        year >= 2023 ~ "Post-COVID (2023+)",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(inflation_rate))
  
  if (nrow(heatmap_data) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "Insufficient data for heatmap"))
  }
  
  # Create the heatmap with proper dimensions and clean layout
  g <- ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = month, y = fct_rev(category_clean), fill = inflation_rate)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.8) +
    # Remove ALL text inside tiles for clean appearance
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
      midpoint = 0, name = "YoY %\nChange",
      limits = c(-10, 20), oob = scales::squish,
      breaks = seq(-10, 20, by = 5)
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~ period, ncol = 1, strip.position = "top") +  # Single column layout
    labs(
      title = "Food Inflation Heatmap: Year-over-Year Changes",
      subtitle = "Seasonal patterns across different time periods",
      x = "Month",
      y = "Food Category",
      caption = "Data: Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      # Fix text sizing and spacing
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, angle = 0, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
      
      # Clean facet labels
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.8),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      
      # Title formatting
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
      
      # Legend positioning
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
      
      # Proper spacing
      panel.spacing.y = unit(1.5, "lines"),
      plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
      
      # Remove grid
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    )
  
  return(g)
}

Price Volatility Analysis
The volatility analysis quantifies price uncertainty through rolling 12-month standard deviations of monthly price changes. Food at home (blue line) exhibits the highest volatility throughout most of the analysis period, with dramatic spikes reaching 0.8% monthly volatility during 2020-2021. This represents unprecedented price unpredictability, far exceeding levels observed during the 2008-2009 financial crisis.
The COVID-19 period marks a clear structural break in price stability across all food categories. Pre-pandemic volatility typically ranged between 0.1-0.3% monthly, while post-COVID levels reached 0.4-0.8%. The synchronized increase across all categories suggests systemic rather than category-specific shocks. By 2024, volatility has declined but remains above pre-pandemic baselines, indicating persistent supply chain fragility.


Show Code
create_ggplot_volatility <- function(data) {
  
  # Get available columns
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  
  if (length(available_cols) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "No data available for volatility analysis"))
  }
  
  # Calculate price changes and rolling volatility
  volatility_data <- data %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      # Monthly price changes
      across(all_of(available_cols), 
             ~ (. / lag(.) - 1) * 100, 
             .names = "{.col}_change")
    )
  
  # Calculate rolling volatility manually for each change column
  change_cols <- paste0(available_cols, "_change")
  
  for (col in change_cols) {
    if (col %in% names(volatility_data)) {
      # Use rollapply instead of rollsd
      volatility_data[[paste0(col, "_vol")]] <- zoo::rollapply(
        volatility_data[[col]], 
        width = 12, 
        FUN = function(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), 
        fill = NA, 
        align = "right",
        partial = FALSE
      )
    }
  }
  
  # Continue with the rest of the analysis
  volatility_data <- volatility_data %>%
    select(date, ends_with("_vol")) %>%
    filter(if_any(ends_with("_vol"), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "category", values_to = "volatility") %>%
    mutate(
      category_clean = case_when(
        str_detect(category, "food_at_home") ~ "Food at Home",
        str_detect(category, "food_away_home") ~ "Food Away from Home",
        str_detect(category, "food_total") ~ "Food Total", 
        str_detect(category, "cpi_all") ~ "Overall CPI",
        TRUE ~ str_remove_all(category, "_change_vol") %>% str_to_title()
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(volatility))
  
  if (nrow(volatility_data) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = "Insufficient data for volatility analysis"))
  }
  
  # Select colors based on available categories
  n_categories <- length(unique(volatility_data$category_clean))
  colors <- c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd")[1:n_categories]
  
  # Create the volatility plot
  g <- ggplot(volatility_data, aes(x = date, y = volatility, color = category_clean)) +
    geom_line(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colors, name = "Category") +
    labs(
      title = "Food Price Volatility: Rolling 12-Month Standard Deviation",
      subtitle = "Measuring price stability across food categories over time",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Monthly Price Change Volatility (%)",
      caption = "Higher volatility = more unpredictable price changes | Smooth lines show trends"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2020-03-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2008-09-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", alpha = 0.7) +
    annotate("text", x = as.Date("2020-06-01"), y = max(volatility_data$volatility, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.9, 
             label = "COVID-19", color = "red", size = 3.5) 
  
  return(g)
}

# Create and display volatility analysis
ggplot_volatility <- create_ggplot_volatility(combined_food_data)
print(ggplot_volatility)









In terms of the food prices part, the data narrative reveals a three-act inflation story. Act I (2010-2019) represents the “Great Moderation” period with stable, predictable food price growth averaging 1-2% annually. Act II (2020-2022) depicts the “Great Disruption”—unprecedented supply chain shocks, monetary expansion, and demand shifts creating multi-decade high inflation rates. Act III (2023-2024) shows “Gradual Normalization”—inflation cooling but price levels permanently elevated, with volatility settling at new, higher equilibrium levels.
The March 2020 inflection point visible across all visualizations marks when pandemic-induced disruptions transformed food markets. Supply chain bottlenecks, labor shortages, and shifting consumption patterns from restaurants to groceries created sustained inflationary pressures. The differential impact between food at home and away from home reflects these consumption shifts and varying supply chain vulnerabilities.
This demonstrates how external shocks can fundamentally alter inflation dynamics, with effects persisting long after initial disruptions subside. The food sector’s essential nature amplified both the immediate impacts and policy responses, creating feedback loops that sustained elevated price growth well into the recovery period.

title: Data Visualization
text:
Housing: When Home Becomes Unaffordable
The housing market tells perhaps the most dramatic story of the past decade, one that transforms the American Dream into an increasingly distant aspiration for millions. What we see in the data is not just a gradual price increase, but a fundamental restructuring of housing affordability that began with the pandemic and shows little sign of reversing. The steady climb of shelter costs from 2010 to 2020 represented a manageable, if concerning, trend. Families could plan, save, and reasonably expect to eventually afford homeownership or rental upgrades.
Then came March 2020, and everything changed. The pandemic didn’t just accelerate existing trends—it shattered them entirely. Housing costs began climbing at rates that outpaced income growth by unprecedented margins. The Federal Reserve’s decision to slash interest rates to near zero, while necessary to prevent economic collapse, inadvertently poured gasoline on the housing fire. Cheap money flowed into real estate markets just as changing work patterns drove families to seek larger homes in different locations. The result was a perfect storm that priced out an entire generation of potential homebuyers and renters alike.


Show Code
# Filter data from 2000 onwards for better storytelling
start_date <- as.Date("2000-01-01")
