title: Data Visualization
section: Monetary Policy: The Double-Edged Sword of Emergency Response
text:
Monetary Policy: The Double-Edged Sword of Emergency Response
The interest rate story reads like a tale of good intentions yielding complicated consequences. When COVID-19 struck, the Federal Reserve acted with unprecedented speed and force, dropping rates to essentially zero within weeks. This decisive action prevented a financial system collapse and kept credit flowing during the darkest days of lockdowns. The data shows this emergency response working exactly as intended—markets stabilized, borrowing costs plummeted, and economic activity gradually resumed.
But the same aggressive accommodation that saved the economy in 2020 became its burden by 2022. As inflation surged beyond anyone’s expectations, the Fed found itself forced into an equally dramatic reversal. The sharp spike in both short and long-term rates visible in our data represents one of the most aggressive tightening cycles in modern monetary history. What makes this story particularly compelling is how it reveals the inherent tension in central banking: the tools powerful enough to rescue an economy in crisis are often too powerful to use without creating new problems down the line.


Show Code
# Combine data
interest_data <- merge(treasury_10y, fed_funds, by = "DATE", all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Treasury_10Y), !is.na(Fed_Funds_Rate)) %>%
  mutate(Yield_Spread = Treasury_10Y - Fed_Funds_Rate)

# Create simple plotly chart
p <- plot_ly(interest_data, x = ~DATE) %>%
  
  # Add Fed Funds Rate
  add_lines(y = ~Fed_Funds_Rate, name = 'Federal Funds Rate', 
            line = list(color = '#E74C3C', width = 3)) %>%
  
  # Add 10-Year Treasury
  add_lines(y = ~Treasury_10Y, name = '10-Year Treasury', 
            line = list(color = '#3498DB', width = 3)) %>%
  
  # Add yield spread
  add_lines(y = ~Yield_Spread, name = 'Yield Spread', 
            line = list(color = '#95A5A6', width = 2, dash = 'dot')) %>%
    
  # Add COVID-19 vertical line
  add_segments(x = as.Date("2020-03-15"), xend = as.Date("2020-03-15"),
               y = 0, yend = 8, 
               line = list(color = "#2C3E50", width = 2, dash = "dash"),
               name = "COVID-19 Pandemic", showlegend = FALSE) %>%
  
  # Simple layout
  layout(
    title = "Monetary Policy Response: Interest Rates During COVID-19 Era",
    xaxis = list(title = "Year"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Interest Rate (%)"),
    hovermode = 'x'
  )

# Display the plot
p

title: Data Visualization
section: Energy: The Wild Card in America’s Inflation Story
text:
Energy: The Wild Card in America’s Inflation Story
Energy prices have always been the wild card in inflation discussions, but the past few years elevated that volatility to extraordinary levels. The gasoline price data captures two massive shocks that bookend the pandemic era—each telling a different story about how global events land in American driveways. The 2020 collapse in energy prices was so severe that oil futures briefly traded negative, a surreal moment when producers literally paid people to take oil off their hands as storage filled up and demand evaporated.
The subsequent recovery and spike following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine demonstrates how quickly energy markets can swing from deflation to inflation. For American families, this volatility translated directly into monthly budget uncertainty. The same commute that cost $40 to fill up in April 2020 suddenly required $70 by March 2022. These aren’t abstract numbers—they represent real choices between filling the gas tank and buying groceries, between driving to work and finding remote alternatives, between maintaining normal routines and fundamentally altering daily life.


Show Code
gas_data <- gasoline_cpi %>%
  filter(DATE >= as.Date("2010-01-01"), !is.na(Gasoline_CPI)) %>%
  mutate(
    YoY_Change = ((Gasoline_CPI / lag(Gasoline_CPI, 12)) - 1) * 100,
    Crisis_Period = case_when(
      DATE >= as.Date("2020-01-01") & DATE <= as.Date("2021-12-31") ~ "COVID-19 Pandemic",
      DATE >= as.Date("2022-01-01") ~ "Post-COVID Inflation",
      TRUE ~ "Normal Period"
    )
  )

# Create subplot with multiple perspectives
energy_plotly <- subplot(
  # Main gasoline CPI plot
  plot_ly(gas_data, x = ~DATE, y = ~Gasoline_CPI, type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = '#E67E22', width = 3), name = 'Gasoline CPI') %>%
    add_markers(data = subset(gas_data, Crisis_Period != "Normal Period"),
                x = ~DATE, y = ~Gasoline_CPI, color = ~Crisis_Period,
                colors = c('#3498DB', '#F39C12'),
                marker = list(size = 4, opacity = 0.7),
                name = 'Crisis Periods') %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(title = "Gasoline CPI")),
  
  # Year-over-year change plot
  plot_ly(gas_data, x = ~DATE, y = ~YoY_Change, type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = '#8E44AD', width = 2), name = 'YoY % Change') %>%
    add_trace(x = range(gas_data$DATE, na.rm = TRUE), y = c(0, 0), 
              type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines',
              line = list(dash = "dash", color = "gray", width = 1),
              name = 'Zero Line', showlegend = FALSE) %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(title = "YoY Change (%)")),
  
  nrows = 2, heights = c(0.7, 0.3), shareX = TRUE
) %>%
  
  layout(
    title = list(text = "<b>Energy Price Volatility During Economic Disruptions</b><br><sub>How COVID-19 and Geopolitical Events Shaped Gasoline Costs</sub>",
                 font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis = list(title = "Year", 
                 tickmode = "linear",
                 dtick = "M24",
                 tickformat = "%Y"),
    showlegend = TRUE,
    annotations = list(
      list(x = as.Date("2020-04-01"), y = 150, text = "Demand Collapse<br>Negative Oil Prices",
           showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "#2C3E50"),
           bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.8)", bordercolor = "#3498DB", borderwidth = 1,
           xref = "x", yref = "y"),
      list(x = as.Date("2022-03-01"), y = 380, text = "Russia-Ukraine<br>Supply Disruption",
           showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "#2C3E50"),
           bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.8)", bordercolor = "#F39C12", borderwidth = 1,
           xref = "x", yref = "y")
    )
  )

# Display the energy plot
energy_plotly






What emerges from the above three visualizations is a portrait of an economy in transition, where traditional patterns have been disrupted and new realities are still taking shape. The COVID-19 pandemic didn’t simply pause normal economic life—it fundamentally altered the relationship between monetary policy, asset prices, and household budgets. Housing became less affordable even as borrowing became cheaper, energy prices swung between extremes with little warning, and families found themselves navigating an economic landscape where past experience provided little guidance for future planning.
These changes represent more than statistical variations; they reflect altered life trajectories, deferred dreams, and adapted expectations. The young couple saving for their first home discovers that their target keeps moving further away. The family planning a budget finds that energy costs make mockery of careful calculations. The retiree on fixed income watches purchasing power erode as the very policies meant to support the economy inflate away their savings.
The data tells us that we’re living through a period where economic policy has become more powerful and more consequential than ever before. The tools that central banks and governments wield can prevent depressions, but they can also accidentally create asset bubbles, affordability crises, and wealth inequality. Understanding these patterns isn’t just an academic exercise—it’s essential for anyone trying to navigate an economy where the old rules no longer seem to apply.

# Load data function
load_fred_csv <- function(file_path, series_name) {

  tryCatch({
    data <- read_csv(file_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
    
    # Handle different CSV formats
    col_names <- names(data)
    date_col <- col_names[grepl("DATE|date|Date", col_names)][1]
    if (is.na(date_col)) date_col <- col_names[1]
    value_col <- col_names[!col_names %in% date_col][1]
    
    data <- data %>% 
      select(date = all_of(date_col), value = all_of(value_col)) %>%
      mutate(
        date = as.Date(date),
        value = as.numeric(as.character(value))
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(value)) %>%
      arrange(date)
    
    return(data)
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("✗ Error loading", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
    return(NULL)
  })
}

# TIME SERIES PLOTS AND COMPONENT IDENTIFICATION

# Create time series objects
create_ts_objects <- function(data) {
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  ts_list <- list()
  
  # Determine start date and frequency
  start_year <- year(min(data$date))
  start_month <- month(min(data$date))
  
  for (col in available_cols) {
    ts_list[[col]] <- ts(data[[col]], start = c(start_year, start_month), frequency = 12)
  }
  
  return(ts_list)
}

ts_data <- create_ts_objects(combined_food_data)

# Function to analyze time series components
analyze_ts_components <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  # Convert to data frame for ggplot
  ts_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )
  
  # Create comprehensive time series plot
  p <- ggplot(ts_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, color = "#ff7f0e", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Time Series Analysis:", series_name),
      subtitle = "Blue line: Original series | Orange line: Trend (LOESS smoothing)",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Consumer Price Index",
      caption = "Data: Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)"
    ) +

# ACF AND PACF ANALYSIS

create_acf_pacf_analysis <- function(ts_obj, series_name, max_lag = 36) {
  
  # Calculate ACF and PACF
  acf_result <- acf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  pacf_result <- pacf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  
  # Create ACF data frame
  acf_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_result$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "ACF (Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Create PACF data frame  
  pacf_df <- data.frame(
    lag = pacf_result$lag[,,1],
    acf = pacf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Combine data
  combined_df <- rbind(acf_df, pacf_df)
  
  # Calculate confidence intervals
  n <- length(ts_obj)
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", size = 0.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Autocorrelation Analysis:", series_name),
      subtitle = "ACF and PACF plots for stationarity and model identification",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Dashed blue lines: 95% confidence intervals | Values outside indicate significant correlation"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max_lag, by = 6))
  
  return(list(plot = p, acf_values = acf_result, pacf_values = pacf_result))
}

# AUGMENTED DICKEY-FULLER STATIONARITY TESTS

perform_adf_tests <- function(ts_data, series_names) {
  
  adf_results <- data.frame(
    Series = character(),
    ADF_Statistic = numeric(),
    P_Value = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_1pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_5pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_10pct = numeric(),
    Is_Stationary_5pct = logical(),
    Is_Stationary_1pct = logical(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  cat("Performing ADF tests...\n")
  
  for(i in 1:length(series_names)) {
    series_name <- series_names[i]
    ts_obj <- ts_data[[series_name]]
    
    # Clean data more thoroughly
    ts_numeric <- as.numeric(ts_obj)  # Convert to numeric first
    ts_clean <- ts_numeric[!is.na(ts_numeric) & is.finite(ts_numeric)]  # Remove NA and infinite values
    
    # Check if we have enough data points
    if (length(ts_clean) < 10) {
      cat("✗ Insufficient data for", series_name, "(", length(ts_clean), "valid points)\n")
      next
    }
    
    # Perform ADF test
    tryCatch({
      adf_test <- adf.test(ts_clean, alternative = "stationary")
      
      display_name <- case_when(
        series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
        series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
        series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
        TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
      )
      
      # Extract critical values properly
      critical_values <- adf_test$parameter
      if (is.null(critical_values) || length(critical_values) == 0) {
        # Use standard critical values if not available
        crit_1pct <- -3.43
        crit_5pct <- -2.86
        crit_10pct <- -2.57
      } else {
        crit_1pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 1, critical_values[1], -3.43)
        crit_5pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 2, critical_values[2], -2.86)
        crit_10pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 3, critical_values[3], -2.57)
      }
      
      adf_results <<- rbind(adf_results, data.frame(
        Series = display_name,
        ADF_Statistic = round(adf_test$statistic, 4),
        P_Value = round(adf_test$p.value, 4),
        Critical_Value_1pct = round(crit_1pct, 4),
        Critical_Value_5pct = round(crit_5pct, 4), 
        Critical_Value_10pct = round(crit_10pct, 4),
        Is_Stationary_5pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.05,
        Is_Stationary_1pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.01
      ))
      
      cat("✓", display_name, "- ADF Statistic:", round(adf_test$statistic, 4), 
          ", p-value:", round(adf_test$p.value, 4), 
          ", Stationary (5%):", adf_test$p.value < 0.05, "\n")
      
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("✗ Error testing", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
      
      # Print diagnostic info
      cat("   Data type:", class(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data length:", length(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data range:", paste(round(range(ts_clean, na.rm = TRUE), 2), collapse = " to "), "\n")
      cat("   First few values:", paste(head(ts_clean, 5), collapse = ", "), "\n")
    })
  }
  
  return(adf_results)
}

# MAKING SERIES STATIONARY 
make_stationary <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI", 
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )

  # First differencing
  diff1 <- diff(ts_obj, differences = 1)
  
  # Test stationarity of differenced series
  adf_test_diff1 <- adf.test(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], alternative = "stationary")
  
  # Create comparison plots - Original vs First Difference
  original_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj),
    series_type = "Original Series"
  )
  
  diff1_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(diff1)),
    value = as.numeric(diff1),
    series_type = "First Difference"
  )
  
  combined_df <- rbind(original_df, diff1_df)
  
  p1 <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Stationarity Transformation:", display_name),
      subtitle = paste("First difference ADF p-value:", round(adf_test_diff1$p.value, 4)),
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value",
      caption = "First differencing removes trend to achieve stationarity"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    )
  
  # ACF comparison - Original vs Differenced
  acf_orig <- acf(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  acf_diff1 <- acf(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  
  acf_orig_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_orig$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_orig$acf[,,1],
    series_type = "Original Series ACF"
  )
  
  acf_diff1_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_diff1$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_diff1$acf[,,1], 
    series_type = "First Difference ACF"
  )
  
  acf_combined <- rbind(acf_orig_df, acf_diff1_df)
  
  n <- length(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)])
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p2 <- ggplot(acf_combined, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("ACF Comparison after Differencing:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparing autocorrelation structure before and after first differencing",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Stationary series should show rapid decay in ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(list(
    comparison_plot = p1,
    acf_comparison = p2,
    differenced_series = diff1,
    adf_result = adf_test_diff1,
    is_stationary_after_diff = adf_test_diff1$p.value < 0.05
  ))
}

perform_ma_smoothing <- function(ts_obj, series_name, windows = c(3, 6, 12, 24)) {

  # Create data frame with original series
  ma_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    original = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )
  
  # Calculate moving averages for different windows
  for(window in windows) {
    ma_values <- SMA(ts_obj, n = window)
    ma_df[[paste0("MA_", window)]] <- as.numeric(ma_values)
  }
  
  # Convert to long format
  ma_long <- ma_df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "ma_type", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(
      ma_type_clean = case_when(
        ma_type == "original" ~ "Original Series",
        TRUE ~ paste("MA(", str_extract(ma_type, "\\d+"), ")", sep = "")
      ),
      line_type = ifelse(ma_type == "original", "Original", "Smoothed"),
      line_size = ifelse(ma_type == "original", 1.2, 1.0)
    )
  
  p <- ggplot(ma_long, aes(x = date, y = value, color = ma_type_clean, size = line_size)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Series Type", option = "plasma") +
    scale_size_identity() +
    labs(
      title = paste("Moving Average Smoothing Analysis:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparison of different smoothing windows to identify underlying patterns",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Index Value",
      caption = "Different MA windows reveal trend (long MA) vs seasonal patterns (short MA)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
    ) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 3))
  
  return(p)
}

# LOG TRANSFORMATION 

check_heteroscedasticity <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  cat("Checking heteroscedasticity for", display_name, "\n")
  
  # Original series
  original_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj),
    log_value = log(as.numeric(ts_obj))
  )
  
  # Calculate residuals from trend
  original_df$trend <- as.numeric(fitted(loess(value ~ as.numeric(date), data = original_df)))
  original_df$residuals <- original_df$value - original_df$trend
  
  # Log residuals
  original_df$log_trend <- as.numeric(fitted(loess(log_value ~ as.numeric(date), data = original_df)))
  original_df$log_residuals <- original_df$log_value - original_df$log_trend
  
  # Create comparison plots
  p1 <- original_df %>%
    select(date, value, log_value) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(value, log_value), names_to = "transformation", values_to = "val") %>%
    mutate(
      transformation_clean = case_when(
        transformation == "value" ~ "Original Series",
        transformation == "log_value" ~ "Log-Transformed Series"
      )
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = val)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ transformation_clean, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Original vs Log-Transformed Series:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Log transformation can stabilize variance if heteroscedasticity is present",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value",
      caption = "Log transformation reduces exponential growth patterns"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    )
  
  # Residuals comparison
  p2 <- original_df %>%
    select(date, residuals, log_residuals) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(residuals, log_residuals), names_to = "residual_type", values_to = "residual") %>%
    mutate(
      residual_type_clean = case_when(
        residual_type == "residuals" ~ "Original Residuals",
        residual_type == "log_residuals" ~ "Log-Transformed Residuals"
      )
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
    geom_line(color = "#d62728", size = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    facet_wrap(~ residual_type_clean, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Residuals Comparison:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparing variance stability between original and log-transformed residuals",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Residuals",
      caption = "More stable residuals (constant variance) suggest appropriate transformation"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightcoral", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  # Calculate variance statistics
  orig_var <- var(original_df$residuals, na.rm = TRUE)
  log_var <- var(original_df$log_residuals, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  cat("  Original residuals variance:", round(orig_var, 4), "\n")
  cat("  Log-transformed residuals variance:", round(log_var, 4), "\n")
  cat("  Variance ratio (log/original):", round(log_var/orig_var, 4), "\n")
  
  return(list(
    comparison_plot = p1,
    residuals_plot = p2,
    log_ts = ts(original_df$log_value, start = start(ts_obj), frequency = frequency(ts_obj)),
    variance_improvement = log_var < orig_var
  ))
}

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Food represents the most immediate and unavoidable component of household cost of living. Unlike discretionary expenses that can be deferred or eliminated, food consumption is fixed—families must eat regardless of price levels. This makes food inflation uniquely impactful on household budgets, particularly for lower-income families who allocate 15-20% of their income to food compared to 10-12% for higher-income households.
The 2010-2024 period captured in this analysis spans a fundamental transition in American food affordability. What began as a decade of predictable, manageable price increases transformed into the most rapid food cost acceleration in forty years. For households operating on fixed or slowly-growing incomes, this wasn’t an abstract economic statistic—it was the difference between filling a grocery cart for $100 versus $130, between weekly restaurant meals becoming monthly luxuries, between comfortable budgeting and constant financial stress.
The time series analysis that follows dissects this transformation through multiple lenses: trend identification reveals the structural break at COVID-19; autocorrelation analysis confirms price increases are permanent rather than reversible; decomposition shows trend dominance over seasonality; and stationarity tests prove each inflation shock resets the baseline permanently higher. Together, these technical findings translate to a simple household reality: food costs won’t return to pre-pandemic levels, budget adjustments must be permanent, and the middle-class consumption patterns of 2019 now require upper-middle-class incomes in 2024.

# Load data function
load_fred_csv <- function(file_path, series_name) {

  tryCatch({
    data <- read_csv(file_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
    
    # Handle different CSV formats
    col_names <- names(data)
    date_col <- col_names[grepl("DATE|date|Date", col_names)][1]
    if (is.na(date_col)) date_col <- col_names[1]
    value_col <- col_names[!col_names %in% date_col][1]
    
    data <- data %>% 
      select(date = all_of(date_col), value = all_of(value_col)) %>%
      mutate(
        date = as.Date(date),
        value = as.numeric(as.character(value))
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(value)) %>%
      arrange(date)
    
    return(data)
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("✗ Error loading", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
    return(NULL)
  })
}

# Create time series objects
create_ts_objects <- function(data) {
  available_cols <- names(data)[names(data) != "date"]
  ts_list <- list()
  
  # Determine start date and frequency
  start_year <- year(min(data$date))
  start_month <- month(min(data$date))
  
  for (col in available_cols) {
    ts_list[[col]] <- ts(data[[col]], start = c(start_year, start_month), frequency = 12)
  }
  
  return(ts_list)
}

ts_data <- create_ts_objects(combined_food_data)

# Function to analyze time series components
analyze_ts_components <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  # Convert to data frame for ggplot
  ts_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )
  
  # Create comprehensive time series plot
  p <- ggplot(ts_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, color = "#ff7f0e", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(

    ) +

    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2020-03-01"), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.6) +
    annotate("text", x = as.Date("2020-06-01"), y = max(ts_df$value) * 0.95,

These time series demonstrate a clear structural break at the COVID-19 pandemic. Pre-2020 food prices followed stable, predictable growth patterns of roughly 2-3% annually. Post-2020, all categories accelerated sharply—groceries increased 30% in four years, equivalent to a decade of pre-pandemic inflation compressed into half the time.
The “Food Away from Home” series shows the steepest and most persistent acceleration, driven by labor market pressures in service industries. The narrowing gap between grocery and restaurant inflation is significant: it eliminated the traditional household buffer of substituting home cooking for dining out during inflationary periods.
What makes this particularly impactful is the synchronization across categories. When food, housing, and energy inflate simultaneously—as shown in the Overall CPI—households cannot offset one expense by reducing another. Lower-income households, which allocate larger budget shares to food, face the greatest pressure with the least flexibility to adjust. The data indicates this is not a temporary price shock but a regime shift. The smooth post-pandemic trajectories suggest inflation became embedded in pricing mechanisms and wage structures. This created sustained real income erosion that required both household behavioral adjustment and monetary policy intervention to address.

All three CPI series exhibit extremely strong positive autocorrelation across all lag periods, as evidenced by the tight clustering of points along the diagonal reference lines. This pattern reveals several key insights:
The high persistence at lag 1 confirms that food prices are highly predictable in the short term—this month’s prices closely predict next month’s. This autocorrelation remains strong even at lag 12, indicating minimal seasonal variation in food inflation. Unlike agricultural commodities that show clear seasonal patterns, processed food CPIs demonstrate smooth, trend-dominated behavior.
The structural break is visible in the color gradients, particularly in “Food at Home” CPI. Points deviate further from the reference line at higher lags (13-16), reflecting the post-pandemic acceleration that disrupted historical price relationships. The pandemic created a regime shift where past values became less reliable predictors of future values. “Food Away from Home” shows the most consistent linearity across all lags, suggesting restaurant prices follow an almost mechanical upward trajectory with minimal volatility. This reflects sticky pricing in service industries where menu adjustments occur infrequently but persistently.
From a household perspective, this strong autocorrelation means food price increases are highly predictable but non-reversible. Unlike energy prices that can spike and retreat, food inflation exhibits a ratchet effect—prices rise and stay elevated. This creates sustained purchasing power erosion rather than temporary shocks, making budget adjustment particularly challenging for households.

# TIME SERIES DECOMPOSITION
decomposition_results <- list()

for (i in 1:length(available_vars)) {
  var_name <- available_vars[i]
  display_name <- case_when(
    var_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    var_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",

    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(var_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  # Try multiplicative first
  tryCatch({
    decomp_mult <- decompose(ts_data[[var_name]], type = "multiplicative")

The multiplicative decomposition reveals that food CPI series are overwhelmingly trend-driven with minimal seasonal or random components. The seasonal fluctuations oscillate within an extremely narrow band (±0.1% around 1.0), indicating food prices exhibit virtually no calendar-based patterns. This contradicts common assumptions about harvest cycles affecting food costs—in reality, modern supply chains and processed food dominance smooth out agricultural seasonality.
The trend component tells the critical story. “Food at Home” shows a decade of stability (2010-2020) followed by sharp acceleration, while “Food Away from Home” demonstrates relentless linear growth throughout. The bend in the trend curves around 2020-2021 quantifies the regime shift: the slope literally doubles, representing a structural change in inflation dynamics rather than cyclical variation.
The remainder component spikes dramatically around 2020-2021 across all three series. These are shocks that the model couldn’t explain through trend or seasonality—supply chain disruptions, pandemic-related demand shifts, and policy interventions. The fact that these “unexplained” deviations remain elevated post-2021 suggests the model struggles with the new inflation regime. What decomposition treats as random error is actually persistent structural change.
For households, the absence of seasonality means no timing strategies exist for reducing food costs. Unlike energy bills that might be reduced by seasonal timing, food inflation is monotonic and unavoidable. The trend dominance confirms that food price increases are systematic and permanent, not temporary fluctuations households can wait out. The remainder spikes show how external shocks create step-changes in the price level that never reverse—each crisis ratchets costs higher without subsequent relief.

# ACF AND PACF ANALYSIS

create_acf_pacf_analysis <- function(ts_obj, series_name, max_lag = 36) {
  
  # Calculate ACF and PACF
  acf_result <- acf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  pacf_result <- pacf(ts_obj, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  
  # Create ACF data frame
  acf_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_result$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "ACF (Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Create PACF data frame  
  pacf_df <- data.frame(
    lag = pacf_result$lag[,,1],
    acf = pacf_result$acf[,,1],
    type = "PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function)"
  )
  
  # Combine data
  combined_df <- rbind(acf_df, pacf_df)
  
  # Calculate confidence intervals
  n <- length(ts_obj)
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", size = 0.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Autocorrelation Analysis:", series_name),
      subtitle = "ACF and PACF plots for stationarity and model identification",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Dashed blue lines: 95% confidence intervals | Values outside indicate significant correlation"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max_lag, by = 6))
  
  return(list(plot = p, acf_values = acf_result, pacf_values = pacf_result))
}

# Create ACF/PACF plots for all series
acf_pacf_results <- list()

for (i in 1:length(available_vars)) {
  var_name <- available_vars[i]
  display_name <- case_when(
    var_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    var_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    var_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(var_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  acf_pacf_results[[var_name]] <- create_acf_pacf_analysis(ts_data[[var_name]], display_name)
  print(acf_pacf_results[[var_name]]$plot)
}























All three series display classic non-stationary characteristics. The ACF shows extremely slow, linear decay rather than rapid exponential decline—autocorrelations remain above 0.5 even at lag 20+. This confirms food prices contain a strong trend component with no mean reversion. The PACF cuts off sharply after lag 1, suggesting an autoregressive process of order 1 with an integrated component (likely ARIMA(1,1,0) or similar). The absence of seasonal spikes at lag 12 in both ACF and PACF is notable—no distinctive patterns appear at annual intervals. This reinforces that food inflation operates independently of agricultural cycles or holiday demand patterns. The pricing mechanisms reflect supply chain intermediation and retailer strategies rather than raw commodity seasonality.
“Food Away from Home” shows the strongest persistence—its ACF decays even more slowly than groceries, and autocorrelations remain significant across all lags shown. This reflects sticky menu pricing in restaurants where costs accumulate over time but price adjustments occur infrequently in large discrete jumps rather than continuous small changes.
For households, this persistence pattern means food price shocks have permanent effects. Unlike stationary processes where deviations eventually revert to mean, these series exhibit unit root behavior—each price increase becomes the new baseline. The high lag-1 autocorrelation (>0.95) indicates prices essentially follow a random walk with drift, making future costs predictable in direction (upward) but not magnitude. Families cannot budget based on historical averages because those averages become obsolete after each inflationary shock.





Show Code
# AUGMENTED DICKEY-FULLER STATIONARITY TESTS

perform_adf_tests <- function(ts_data, series_names) {
  
  adf_results <- data.frame(
    Series = character(),
    ADF_Statistic = numeric(),
    P_Value = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_1pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_5pct = numeric(),
    Critical_Value_10pct = numeric(),
    Is_Stationary_5pct = logical(),
    Is_Stationary_1pct = logical(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  cat("Performing ADF tests...\n")
  
  for(i in 1:length(series_names)) {
    series_name <- series_names[i]
    ts_obj <- ts_data[[series_name]]
    
    # Clean data more thoroughly
    ts_numeric <- as.numeric(ts_obj)  # Convert to numeric first
    ts_clean <- ts_numeric[!is.na(ts_numeric) & is.finite(ts_numeric)]  # Remove NA and infinite values
    
    # Check if we have enough data points
    if (length(ts_clean) < 10) {
      cat("✗ Insufficient data for", series_name, "(", length(ts_clean), "valid points)\n")
      next
    }
    
    # Perform ADF test
    tryCatch({
      adf_test <- adf.test(ts_clean, alternative = "stationary")
      
      display_name <- case_when(
        series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
        series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
        series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
        TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
      )
      
      # Extract critical values properly
      critical_values <- adf_test$parameter
      if (is.null(critical_values) || length(critical_values) == 0) {
        # Use standard critical values if not available
        crit_1pct <- -3.43
        crit_5pct <- -2.86
        crit_10pct <- -2.57
      } else {
        crit_1pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 1, critical_values[1], -3.43)
        crit_5pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 2, critical_values[2], -2.86)
        crit_10pct <- ifelse(length(critical_values) >= 3, critical_values[3], -2.57)
      }
      
      adf_results <<- rbind(adf_results, data.frame(
        Series = display_name,
        ADF_Statistic = round(adf_test$statistic, 4),
        P_Value = round(adf_test$p.value, 4),
        Critical_Value_1pct = round(crit_1pct, 4),
        Critical_Value_5pct = round(crit_5pct, 4), 
        Critical_Value_10pct = round(crit_10pct, 4),
        Is_Stationary_5pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.05,
        Is_Stationary_1pct = adf_test$p.value < 0.01
      ))
      
      cat("✓", display_name, "- ADF Statistic:", round(adf_test$statistic, 4), 
          ", p-value:", round(adf_test$p.value, 4), 
          ", Stationary (5%):", adf_test$p.value < 0.05, "\n")
      
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("✗ Error testing", series_name, ":", e$message, "\n")
      
      # Print diagnostic info
      cat("   Data type:", class(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data length:", length(ts_clean), "\n")
      cat("   Data range:", paste(round(range(ts_clean, na.rm = TRUE), 2), collapse = " to "), "\n")
      cat("   First few values:", paste(head(ts_clean, 5), collapse = ", "), "\n")
    })
  }
  
  return(adf_results)
}

# Perform ADF tests 
adf_results <- perform_adf_tests(ts_data, available_vars)

All three series fail stationarity tests with p-values near 1.0, confirming unit root presence. Food prices follow random walks—shocks are permanent, not temporary. Differencing is required before modeling. For households: price increases never reverse, each inflation episode permanently resets the cost baseline.

# MAKING SERIES STATIONARY 
make_stationary <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI", 
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )

  # First differencing
  diff1 <- diff(ts_obj, differences = 1)
  
  # Test stationarity of differenced series
  adf_test_diff1 <- adf.test(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], alternative = "stationary")
  
  # Create comparison plots - Original vs First Difference
  original_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj),
    series_type = "Original Series"
  )
  
  diff1_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(diff1)),
    value = as.numeric(diff1),
    series_type = "First Difference"
  )
  
  combined_df <- rbind(original_df, diff1_df)
  
  p1 <- ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Stationarity Transformation:", display_name),
      subtitle = paste("First difference ADF p-value:", round(adf_test_diff1$p.value, 4)),
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value",
      caption = "First differencing removes trend to achieve stationarity"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    )
  
  # ACF comparison - Original vs Differenced
  acf_orig <- acf(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  acf_diff1 <- acf(diff1[!is.na(diff1)], lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)
  
  acf_orig_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_orig$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_orig$acf[,,1],
    series_type = "Original Series ACF"
  )
  
  acf_diff1_df <- data.frame(
    lag = acf_diff1$lag[,,1],
    acf = acf_diff1$acf[,,1], 
    series_type = "First Difference ACF"
  )
  
  acf_combined <- rbind(acf_orig_df, acf_diff1_df)
  
  n <- length(ts_obj[!is.na(ts_obj)])
  ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)
  
  p2 <- ggplot(acf_combined, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 2) +
    facet_wrap(~ series_type, ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("ACF Comparison after Differencing:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparing autocorrelation structure before and after first differencing",
      x = "Lag",
      y = "Autocorrelation",
      caption = "Stationary series should show rapid decay in ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", alpha = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(list(
    comparison_plot = p1,
    acf_comparison = p2,
    differenced_series = diff1,
    adf_result = adf_test_diff1,
    is_stationary_after_diff = adf_test_diff1$p.value < 0.05
  ))
}

perform_ma_smoothing <- function(ts_obj, series_name, windows = c(3, 6, 12, 24)) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)", 
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  cat("Creating MA smoothing for", display_name, "with windows:", paste(windows, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  
  # Create data frame with original series
  ma_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    original = as.numeric(ts_obj)
  )
  
  # Calculate moving averages for different windows
  for(window in windows) {
    ma_values <- SMA(ts_obj, n = window)
    ma_df[[paste0("MA_", window)]] <- as.numeric(ma_values)
  }
  
  # Convert to long format
  ma_long <- ma_df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "ma_type", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(
      ma_type_clean = case_when(
        ma_type == "original" ~ "Original Series",
        TRUE ~ paste("MA(", str_extract(ma_type, "\\d+"), ")", sep = "")
      ),
      line_type = ifelse(ma_type == "original", "Original", "Smoothed"),
      line_size = ifelse(ma_type == "original", 1.2, 1.0)
    )
  
  p <- ggplot(ma_long, aes(x = date, y = value, color = ma_type_clean, size = line_size)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Series Type", option = "plasma") +
    scale_size_identity() +
    labs(
      title = paste("Moving Average Smoothing Analysis:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparison of different smoothing windows to identify underlying patterns",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Index Value",
      caption = "Different MA windows reveal trend (long MA) vs seasonal patterns (short MA)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
    ) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 3))
  
  return(p)
}

check_heteroscedasticity <- function(ts_obj, series_name) {
  
  display_name <- case_when(
    series_name == "food_at_home" ~ "Food at Home CPI",
    series_name == "food_away_home" ~ "Food Away from Home CPI",
    series_name == "cpi_all" ~ "Overall CPI (All Items)",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(series_name, "_", " "))
  )
  
  cat("Checking heteroscedasticity for", display_name, "\n")
  
  # Original series
  original_df <- data.frame(
    date = as.Date(time(ts_obj)),
    value = as.numeric(ts_obj),
    log_value = log(as.numeric(ts_obj))
  )
  
  # Calculate residuals from trend
  original_df$trend <- as.numeric(fitted(loess(value ~ as.numeric(date), data = original_df)))
  original_df$residuals <- original_df$value - original_df$trend
  
  # Log residuals
  original_df$log_trend <- as.numeric(fitted(loess(log_value ~ as.numeric(date), data = original_df)))
  original_df$log_residuals <- original_df$log_value - original_df$log_trend
  
  # Create comparison plots
  p1 <- original_df %>%
    select(date, value, log_value) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(value, log_value), names_to = "transformation", values_to = "val") %>%
    mutate(
      transformation_clean = case_when(
        transformation == "value" ~ "Original Series",
        transformation == "log_value" ~ "Log-Transformed Series"
      )
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = val)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ transformation_clean, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Original vs Log-Transformed Series:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Log transformation can stabilize variance if heteroscedasticity is present",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value",
      caption = "Log transformation reduces exponential growth patterns"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")
    )
  
  # Residuals comparison
  p2 <- original_df %>%
    select(date, residuals, log_residuals) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(residuals, log_residuals), names_to = "residual_type", values_to = "residual") %>%
    mutate(
      residual_type_clean = case_when(
        residual_type == "residuals" ~ "Original Residuals",
        residual_type == "log_residuals" ~ "Log-Transformed Residuals"
      )
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
    geom_line(color = "#d62728", size = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    facet_wrap(~ residual_type_clean, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Residuals Comparison:", display_name),
      subtitle = "Comparing variance stability between original and log-transformed residuals",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Residuals",
      caption = "More stable residuals (constant variance) suggest appropriate transformation"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightcoral", alpha = 0.3),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  # Calculate variance statistics
  orig_var <- var(original_df$residuals, na.rm = TRUE)
  log_var <- var(original_df$log_residuals, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  cat("  Original residuals variance:", round(orig_var, 4), "\n")
  cat("  Log-transformed residuals variance:", round(log_var, 4), "\n")
  cat("  Variance ratio (log/original):", round(log_var/orig_var, 4), "\n")
  
  return(list(
    comparison_plot = p1,
    residuals_plot = p2,
    log_ts = ts(original_df$log_value, start = start(ts_obj), frequency = frequency(ts_obj)),
    variance_improvement = log_var < orig_var
  ))
}

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
section: Interest Rates and Household Borrowing Costs: The Hidden Inflation Multiplier
text:
Interest Rates and Household Borrowing Costs: The Hidden Inflation Multiplier
Interest rates represent the price of money itself—the cost households pay to bridge the gap between current income and major life purchases. Unlike food or energy prices that directly extract dollars from monthly budgets, interest rates determine whether families can access homeownership, vehicle ownership, and higher education at all. A mortgage rate increase from 3% to 7% doesn’t just raise monthly payments—it prices millions out of the housing market entirely, forcing them into rental markets where they face the combined burden of rising rents plus inability to build home equity.
The 2020-2024 period captured an unprecedented interest rate whipsaw: emergency accommodation drove rates to historic lows, creating a brief window for refinancing and purchases, followed by the fastest tightening cycle in four decades. This volatility transformed interest rates from a stable background parameter families could plan around into an unpredictable variable that invalidated multi-year financial strategies within months. The time series analysis reveals how policy-driven rate regimes exhibit high persistence within periods but abrupt transitions between them—creating a binary environment where timing luck matters more than prudent planning, and where yesterday’s 3% mortgage becomes today’s unobtainable dream while housing prices refuse to adjust downward.


Show Code
treasury_10y <- read_csv("./data/DGS10.csv")
fed_funds <- read_csv("./data/FEDFUNDS.csv")

# Rename columns
names(treasury_10y) <- c("date", "treasury_rate")
names(fed_funds) <- c("date", "fed_rate")

# Convert dates
treasury_10y$date <- as.Date(treasury_10y$date)
fed_funds$date <- as.Date(fed_funds$date)

# Clean data
treasury_clean <- treasury_10y %>% filter(!is.na(treasury_rate))
fed_clean <- fed_funds %>% filter(!is.na(fed_rate))

# Find common date range
common_start <- max(min(treasury_clean$date), min(fed_clean$date))
common_end <- min(max(treasury_clean$date), max(fed_clean$date))

treasury_clean <- treasury_clean %>% filter(date >= common_start & date <= common_end)
fed_clean <- fed_clean %>% filter(date >= common_start & date <= common_end)

# Convert to time series
treasury_ts <- ts(treasury_clean$treasury_rate, 
                 start = c(year(common_start), month(common_start)), 
                 frequency = 12)
fed_ts <- ts(fed_clean$fed_rate, 
            start = c(year(common_start), month(common_start)), 
            frequency = 12)
# TIME SERIES PLOTS
p1 <- autoplot(treasury_ts) +
  ggtitle("10-Year Treasury Rate (1954-2024)") +
  xlab("Year") +
  ylab("Interest Rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))

p2 <- autoplot(fed_ts) +
  ggtitle("Federal Funds Rate (1954-2024)") +
  xlab("Year") +
  ylab("Interest Rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 1)









Show Code
combined_data <- data.frame(
  date = treasury_clean$date,
  treasury = treasury_clean$treasury_rate,
  fed_funds = fed_clean$fed_rate
)

p3 <- ggplot(combined_data, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = treasury, color = "10-Year Treasury"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fed_funds, color = "Federal Funds Rate"), size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("10-Year Treasury" = "#3498DB", 
                               "Federal Funds Rate" = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Interest Rate Environment: Policy vs Market Dynamics (1954-2024)",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Interest Rate (%)",
       color = "Rate Type") +
  theme_minimal() +

        legend.position = "bottom")

The Federal Funds Rate shows the Fed’s dramatic COVID-19 response: near-zero rates (March 2020) followed by the fastest tightening cycle in decades (2022-2023), reaching 5.5%. This whipsaw movement directly impacted household borrowing costs—mortgage rates, credit cards, auto loans all tracked the policy shift.
The 10-Year Treasury Rate reflects market expectations rather than Fed policy. Its more gradual movement and current decline (despite elevated Fed rates) suggests markets anticipate economic weakness forcing eventual rate cuts. The gap between policy rates and market rates reveals skepticism about sustainability of restrictive policy.
Household Impact: The 2020-2021 ultra-low rates enabled some families to refinance mortgages at sub-3% (permanent monthly payment reductions). However, the subsequent spike to 7%+ mortgage rates by 2023 priced millions out of homeownership entirely. For existing homeowners with fixed-rate mortgages, this created “lock-in” effects—unable to move without trading 3% rates for 7%+ rates. For renters and new buyers, the dual pressure of elevated home prices (from the low-rate boom) plus high borrowing costs created unprecedented affordability barriers. Credit card rates exceeding 20% added pressure to households already stretched by food and housing inflation.

Lag Plot Analysis: Interest Rate Autocorrelation and Policy Regimes

print(p_lag_fed)









10-Year Treasury: Strong positive correlation at lag 1 weakens progressively through lag 16. The color clustering reveals regime-dependent behavior—tight bunching during stable periods, scattered dispersion during transition phases (visible as color separation at lags 5-8). No seasonal patterns at lag 12, confirming interest rates are policy/cycle-driven, not calendar-driven.
Federal Funds Rate: Exhibits distinct structural breaks. Lag 1-4 shows bifurcation—zero-rate period (2010-2015, 2020-2021) clusters at origin while normal periods follow diagonal. At longer lags (13-16), horizontal banding appears at 0% and 5%+ levels, reflecting the Fed’s tendency to hold rates constant for extended periods rather than adjusting continuously. This “staircase” behavior creates household uncertainty—borrowing costs jump suddenly then freeze, making financial planning difficult.
Household Implications: The weak autocorrelation at longer lags means past rates poorly predict future rates beyond 6-12 months. Unlike food inflation’s high persistence, interest rate regimes can shift abruptly due to policy changes. Families refinancing mortgages or taking variable-rate debt face unpredictable cost trajectories—rates that seem stable can spike within months during policy pivots.


Decomposition Analysis: Interest Rates Driven by Policy, Not Seasons


Show Code
# DECOMPOSITION

tryCatch({
  treasury_decomp <- decompose(treasury_ts, type = "additive")
  
  p_decomp_treasury <- autoplot(treasury_decomp) +
    ggtitle("10-Year Treasury Rate: Time Series Decomposition") +
    labs(subtitle = "Decomposition Type: Additive",
         x = "Time",
         y = "Value") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
  
  print(p_decomp_treasury)
}, error = function(e) {})









Show Code
tryCatch({
  fed_decomp <- decompose(fed_ts, type = "additive")
  
  p_decomp_fed <- autoplot(fed_decomp) +
    ggtitle("Federal Funds Rate: Time Series Decomposition") +
    labs(subtitle = "Decomposition Type: Additive",

         y = "Value") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))

}, error = function(e) {})









10-Year Treasury: Trend dominates—showing long business cycles (2010s decline, 2020s rise). Seasonal component is negligible (±0.15%), confirming interest rates have zero calendar-based patterns. Remainder spikes during 2020-2023 reflect COVID-19 shock and inflation surprise—volatility the model couldn’t explain through trend alone.
Federal Funds Rate: Exhibits pure step-function trend—flat at 0% (2010-2015, 2020-2021), gradual rise (2016-2019), vertical jump to 5%+ (2022-2023). Seasonal component is virtually flat, remainder concentrated around policy shift periods. This “staircase” pattern reflects deliberate Fed decisions rather than gradual market evolution.
Comparison: Treasury rates show smooth cyclical trends; Fed rates show abrupt regime changes. The remainder components tell different stories—Treasury volatility reflects market uncertainty, Fed remainder reflects implementation lags between policy announcements and actual rate changes.
Household Impact: Zero seasonality means no timing advantage for major borrowing decisions. The large remainder spikes during 2020-2023 quantify household uncertainty—borrowing costs deviated massively from predictable patterns, making financial planning nearly impossible during the policy whipsaw period.


ACF/PACF Analysis: Non-Stationarity and Policy Persistence


Show Code
# ACF AND PACF
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
acf(treasury_ts, lag.max = 40, main = "10-Year Treasury Rate - ACF")
pacf(treasury_ts, lag.max = 40, main = "10-Year Treasury Rate - PACF")
acf(fed_ts, lag.max = 40, main = "Federal Funds Rate - ACF")
pacf(fed_ts, lag.max = 40, main = "Federal Funds Rate - PACF")









Show Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Both series show clear non-stationarity: ACF decays slowly rather than dropping sharply, with significant autocorrelation persisting beyond 30 lags. PACF cuts off after lag 1-2, suggesting AR(1) or AR(2) processes with integrated components.
10-Year Treasury: Gradual ACF decay reflects smooth cyclical behavior driven by business cycles and inflation expectations. The negative autocorrelation appearing around lag 18-20 suggests mean-reverting tendencies at longer horizons—markets eventually expect rates to return toward long-run equilibrium.
Federal Funds Rate: Extremely high persistence (ACF>0.8 through lag 15) reflects Fed policy inertia—rates stay constant for extended periods. The sharp PACF cutoff after lag 1 indicates current rates almost perfectly predict next month’s rates, confirming the staircase pattern where the Fed holds rates steady between discrete adjustment cycles.
Household Implications: High persistence means rate changes, once implemented, persist for years. Families refinancing during low-rate windows locked in decade-long savings. Conversely, those borrowing during high-rate periods face extended periods of elevated costs. The slow ACF decay confirms interest rate regimes are sticky—unlike volatile asset prices, borrowing cost environments change infrequently but dramatically, requiring long-term financial planning rather than short-term timing strategies.


Differencing Results: Achieving Stationarity


Show Code

fed_adf <- adf.test(fed_ts, alternative = "stationary")

fed_diff <- diff(fed_ts, differences = 1)

plot(treasury_diff, main = "First Differenced 10-Year Treasury Rate", ylab = "Change (%)")

plot(fed_diff, main = "First Differenced Federal Funds Rate", ylab = "Change (%)")

pacf(fed_diff, lag.max = 40, main = "Differenced Fed Funds Rate - PACF")

fed_diff_adf <- adf.test(fed_diff, alternative = "stationary")


Visual Transformation: Original series show clear trends and non-stationarity. Differenced series fluctuate around zero with no visible drift—successful stationarity transformation. Treasury rate differences show consistent volatility; Fed rate differences reveal the 2020 collapse and 2022 spike as extreme outliers.
ACF/PACF Confirmation: Post-differencing, both series show rapid ACF decay to near-zero within 3-5 lags—classic stationary behavior. The Fed Funds ACF still shows slight elevated correlation at early lags due to the stepped adjustment pattern, but overall the unit root is eliminated. Treasury vs. Fed Dynamics: Differenced Treasury rates exhibit normally-distributed month-to-month changes (±0.3%), reflecting continuous market adjustment. Differenced Fed rates show long periods near zero punctuated by extreme spikes (±0.5%), confirming discrete policy adjustments rather than gradual evolution.
Household Implications: The differenced series represent rate change volatility—how unpredictably borrowing costs shift month-to-month. Treasury volatility averaged ±0.15% monthly but spiked to ±0.6% during 2020-2022, quantifying the uncertainty households faced. The 2020-2022 period shows unprecedented rate-change volatility in both series, making multi-year financial planning (mortgages, car loans, college financing) exceptionally difficult as future borrowing costs became unpredictable even 6-12 months forward.


Moving Average Smoothing


Show Code
ma_windows <- c(3, 6, 12, 24, 36)

calculate_ma <- function(ts_data, window) {
  ma_result <- stats::filter(ts_data, rep(1/window, window), sides = 2)
  return(ma_result)
}

treasury_ma <- lapply(ma_windows, function(w) calculate_ma(treasury_ts, w))
names(treasury_ma) <- paste("MA", ma_windows, sep = "_")

fed_ma <- lapply(ma_windows, function(w) calculate_ma(fed_ts, w))
names(fed_ma) <- paste("MA", ma_windows, sep = "_")

create_ma_plot <- function(original_ts, ma_list, title_prefix) {
  time_index <- time(original_ts)
  
  plot_data <- data.frame(
    time = as.numeric(time_index),
    original = as.numeric(original_ts)
  )
  
  for(i in 1:length(ma_list)) {
    plot_data[[names(ma_list)[i]]] <- as.numeric(ma_list[[i]])
  }
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = time)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = original, color = "Original"), alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_line(aes(y = MA_3, color = "MA(3)"), size = 0.8) +
    geom_line(aes(y = MA_6, color = "MA(6)"), size = 0.8) +
    geom_line(aes(y = MA_12, color = "MA(12)"), size = 1) +
    geom_line(aes(y = MA_24, color = "MA(24)"), size = 1) +
    geom_line(aes(y = MA_36, color = "MA(36)"), size = 1.2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      "Original" = "gray70",
      "MA(3)" = "#E74C3C",
      "MA(6)" = "#F39C12", 
      "MA(12)" = "#3498DB",
      "MA(24)" = "#2ECC71",
      "MA(36)" = "#9B59B6"
    )) +
    labs(title = paste(title_prefix, "- Moving Average Smoothing"),
         x = "Year",
         y = "Interest Rate (%)",
         color = "Series") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  
  return(p)
}

treasury_ma_plot <- create_ma_plot(treasury_ts, treasury_ma, "10-Year Treasury Rate")
fed_ma_plot <- create_ma_plot(fed_ts, fed_ma, "Federal Funds Rate")

print(treasury_ma_plot)









Show Code
print(fed_ma_plot)









10-Year Treasury: All MA windows converge closely during 2010-2019, confirming stable rate environment. Post-2020 shows dramatic divergence—short MAs (3, 6) capture the rapid collapse to 0.7% and subsequent spike to 4.5%, while MA36 lags significantly. By 2024, MAs reconverge around 4%, but the gap during 2020-2023 quantifies the unprecedented volatility households faced.
Federal Funds Rate: The staircase pattern remains visible even in long MAs. MA36 completely smooths out the 2016-2019 gradual rise, showing only the zero-rate plateaus (2010-2015, 2020-2021) and the 2022-2023 vertical jump. Short MAs track the discrete policy steps, while long MAs reveal just two regimes: accommodation versus restriction, with almost no middle ground.
Volatility Contrast: Treasury MA divergence during 2020-2023 exceeded any prior period—the gap between MA3 and MA36 reached 2 percentage points, reflecting genuine market uncertainty. Fed rate MAs show less divergence because changes were deliberate policy steps, not market reactions.
Household Impact: The Treasury MA spread during 2020-2023 measures the unpredictability premium households paid. When 3-month and 36-month moving averages diverge by 2%, long-term financial planning becomes impossible—today’s mortgage rate provides zero information about refinancing options 2-3 years forward. The subsequent reconvergence offers no relief because rates stabilized at elevated levels, not pre-pandemic baselines.

as_monthly_ts <- function(x) {

  if (inherits(x, "ts")) {
    x <- stats::na.omit(x)
    ts(as.numeric(x), start = start(x), frequency = ifelse(frequency(x) > 1, frequency(x), 12))
  } else {

safe_arima_fit <- function(x, p, d, q, include_drift = (d == 1)) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "ML"),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "CSS-ML"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
  }
  fit
}

manual_arima_grid <- function(x, d = 1, pmax = 4, qmax = 4) {
  rows <- vector("list", (pmax + 1) * (qmax + 1))
  errs <- vector("list", length(rows))
  k <- 1
  for (p in 0:pmax) {
    for (q in 0:qmax) {
      fit <- safe_arima_fit(x, p, d, q)
      if (is.null(fit)) {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = NA_real_, BIC = NA_real_, AICc = NA_real_,
                                status = "failed")
      } else {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = AIC(fit),
                                BIC = BIC(fit),
                                AICc = if (!is.null(fit$aicc)) fit$aicc else NA_real_,
                                status = "ok")
      }
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  out <- out[order(out$BIC), ]
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

as_monthly_ts <- function(x) {

  if (inherits(x, "ts")) {
    x <- stats::na.omit(x)
    ts(as.numeric(x), start = start(x), frequency = ifelse(frequency(x) > 1, frequency(x), 12))
  } else {
    x <- stats::na.omit(as.numeric(x))
    ts(x, frequency = 12)
  }
}

safe_arima_fit <- function(x, p, d, q, include_drift = (d == 1)) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "ML"),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "CSS-ML"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
  }
  fit
}

manual_arima_grid <- function(x, d = 1, pmax = 4, qmax = 4) {
  rows <- vector("list", (pmax + 1) * (qmax + 1))
  errs <- vector("list", length(rows))
  k <- 1
  for (p in 0:pmax) {
    for (q in 0:qmax) {
      fit <- safe_arima_fit(x, p, d, q)
      if (is.null(fit)) {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = NA_real_, BIC = NA_real_, AICc = NA_real_,
                                status = "failed")
      } else {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = AIC(fit),
                                BIC = BIC(fit),
                                AICc = if (!is.null(fit$aicc)) fit$aicc else NA_real_,
                                status = "ok")
      }
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  out <- out[order(out$BIC), ]
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

as_monthly_ts <- function(x) {

  if (inherits(x, "ts")) {
    x <- stats::na.omit(x)
    ts(as.numeric(x), start = start(x), frequency = ifelse(frequency(x) > 1, frequency(x), 12))
  } else {
    x <- stats::na.omit(as.numeric(x))
    ts(x, frequency = 12)
  }
}

safe_arima_fit <- function(x, p, d, q, include_drift = (d == 1)) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "ML"),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "CSS-ML"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
  }
  fit
}

manual_arima_grid <- function(x, d = 1, pmax = 4, qmax = 4) {
  rows <- vector("list", (pmax + 1) * (qmax + 1))
  errs <- vector("list", length(rows))
  k <- 1
  for (p in 0:pmax) {
    for (q in 0:qmax) {
      fit <- safe_arima_fit(x, p, d, q)
      if (is.null(fit)) {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = NA_real_, BIC = NA_real_, AICc = NA_real_,
                                status = "failed")
      } else {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = AIC(fit),
                                BIC = BIC(fit),
                                AICc = if (!is.null(fit$aicc)) fit$aicc else NA_real_,
                                status = "ok")
      }
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  out <- out[order(out$BIC), ]
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

as_monthly_ts <- function(x) {

  if (inherits(x, "ts")) {
    x <- stats::na.omit(x)
    ts(as.numeric(x), start = start(x), frequency = ifelse(frequency(x) > 1, frequency(x), 12))
  } else {
    x <- stats::na.omit(as.numeric(x))
    ts(x, frequency = 12)
  }
}

safe_arima_fit <- function(x, p, d, q, include_drift = (d == 1)) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "ML"),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      Arima(x, order = c(p, d, q), include.drift = include_drift, method = "CSS-ML"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
  }
  fit
}

manual_arima_grid <- function(x, d = 1, pmax = 4, qmax = 4) {
  rows <- vector("list", (pmax + 1) * (qmax + 1))
  errs <- vector("list", length(rows))
  k <- 1
  for (p in 0:pmax) {
    for (q in 0:qmax) {
      fit <- safe_arima_fit(x, p, d, q)
      if (is.null(fit)) {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = NA_real_, BIC = NA_real_, AICc = NA_real_,
                                status = "failed")
      } else {
        rows[[k]] <- data.frame(p = p, d = d, q = q,
                                AIC = AIC(fit),
                                BIC = BIC(fit),
                                AICc = if (!is.null(fit$aicc)) fit$aicc else NA_real_,
                                status = "ok")
      }
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  out <- out[order(out$BIC), ]
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

title: Data Sources
text:
2) Shelter Costs (rent, OER, market rents)
What to study: CPI shelter’s stickiness; market rent → CPI lags; mortgage rate environment.
Sources:

BLS CPI: Shelter, Rent of primary residence, Owners’ equivalent rent
Core measures used in headline/core CPI; anchor for official shelter inflation.
Zillow/Apartment List Rent Index (monthly) | Apartment List
High-frequency market rents to gauge leads/lags relative to CPI shelter.
Freddie Mac PMMS mortgage rates (weekly)
Rate environment shaping housing demand and landlord financing costs.
S&P/Case-Shiller Home Price (monthly)
Asset-price backdrop informing housing tightness and rent dynamics.




Figure 2.3: Housing Cost From Freddie Mac Over Time





3) Utilities & Home Energy (electricity, gas, water/sewer/trash)
What to study: Seasonal structure; energy shocks; weather load (HDD/CDD).
Sources:

BLS CPI: Electricity, Utility (piped) gas service, Water/sewer/trash
Consumer price outcomes for utility categories.
EIA: retail electricity & natural gas prices/consumption
Supply-side prices/usage to connect wholesale shocks to retail bills.
NOAA: HDD/CDD and temperature time series
Weather load metrics to explain seasonal and shock-driven demand.




Figure 2.4: U.S. Regular Gasoline Prices Over Time





4) Transportation & Fuel (gasoline, transit, auto services)
What to study: Oil → gasoline pass-through; asymmetry (rocket-feather); service costs.
Sources:

BLS CPI: Gasoline, Transportation services (e.g., insurance, maintenance)
End-user prices for fuel and transport-related services.
EIA: WTI/Brent, retail gasoline (weekly)
Upstream crude and retail fuel to measure pass-through and timing.
BLS PPI for upstream costs
Producer-level cost pressures feeding into consumer services.




5) Household Services (childcare, health out-of-pocket, education, internet/phone)
What to study: Price stickiness; trend vs cyclical; income sensitivity.
Sources:

BLS CPI detailed services (monthly)
Granular service categories to assess persistence of core inflation.
FRED health/education price indexes
Curated time series (healthcare, tuition, telecom) for long-run context.




6) Regional & Demographic Heterogeneity
What to study: Metro/regional CPI; urban vs non-urban; distributional burden.
Sources:

BLS regional CPI & selected metro indexes
Official regional inflation measures to compare geography.
BEA regional price parity (annual with trend context)
Relative price levels across states/MSAs to complement CPI growth rates.
CPS micro indicators (for demographic overlays)
Household characteristics enabling distributional analysis.




Figure 2.5: Regional CPI & Selected Indexes Over Time





7) Expectations & Sentiment
What to study: Do inflation expectations predict category moves?
Sources:

NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (monthly)
Household inflation expectations and uncertainty.
University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers
Sentiment and expected price changes for near-term demand signals.
Market-based inflation compensation (breakevens via FRED)
Investor-implied inflation expectations from TIPS markets.




8) Supply Chains & Commodities
What to study: Import prices, shipping costs, ag/industrial commodities → retail.
Sources:

BLS Import/Export Price Indexes
Border prices to assess external cost pressures and pass-through.
FAO Food Price Index
Global agricultural price benchmark for U.S. food categories.
Freight indices (e.g., Drewry/FBX—if accessible)
Shipping cost gauge for supply-chain tightness/bottlenecks.




Figure 2.6: U.S. Import and Export Price Indexes Over Time





9) Policy Episodes & Regime Shifts (e.g., COVID-19, tightening cycles)
What to study: Before/after analyses, breaks, and time-varying pass-through.
Sources:

Federal Reserve monetary policy timeline
Dates/cycles for policy shocks and guidance pivots.
Fiscal policy events (Treasury/Congressional sources)
Stimulus, tax, and transfer programs shaping demand and incomes.
CPI category histories (BLS)
Baseline to identify structural breaks and regime changes.




10) Forecasts & Scenarios (12–24 months)
What to study: Conditional paths: if core inflation/energy follows a path, where do costs go?
Sources:

Consensus forecasts (e.g., Survey of Professional Forecasters)
External benchmarks to anchor scenario ranges.
EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook
Energy price paths to condition fuel/utility scenarios.
Internal model outputs (produced later)
